#40194 7 2004-12-09T12:40:26Z iangb
Sometimes you can get lucky just by putting objects/tiles in an order that looks promising, then pressing play and seeing what happens. However, normally I start with a little bit of planning off-screen, for maybe the first 10 seconds or so (for a great example see More Thwump Power - the first decent, rise and loop was all planned on paper beforehand. Then, see where your ninja ends up and add another feature to shunt him (or her??) on a bit more. Keep going until you run out of ideas. Never be afraid to try something new - who would know if it went wrong!! If possible, try to get a section the ninja passes through repeatedly with different results - again the map is (quite) a good example. Try to keep up the pace by introducing enemies/close calls, but remember that if you add too many the lag will ruin the level. Thats all... I think. Have fun!!

#41492 22 2004-12-16T14:04:17Z iangb
yup - suki is right (again). Centrepetal force is basically the name given to any force, (be it gravity, tension in a string, or friction between the turning car's wheels and the road) that acts TOWARDS the point around which a body turns - it is this force which causes the body to turn. So technically, i guess, centrepetal force doesn't exist either - it is merely the name given to whatever force is involved in circular motion.

Centrefugal force is non-existant - the reason you feel a 'pull' outward when you are in a car going round a bend is that your mass 'wants' *wince* to go in a straight line, in accordance with the wonderful laws of Newton & co. It was orginally invented by the slow-of-thought who used it to explain why objects move in a straight line - they imagened the centrepetal force being there constantly, and centrefugal force counteracting it to make a straight line. Actually it is the opposite - there are no forces involved in a straight line - that's the point.

I think that all makes sense

#47139 2 2005-01-21T10:00:45Z iangb
the dot product as I understand it:

If you have two vectors (not position vectors), they can be called a and b but they stand for the movement you have to do. eg: a = 5i +6j, and b = 2i + 3j. a + b = (5 + 2)i + (6 + 3)j = 7i + 9j, so from the origin you go 7 across and 9 up.

the dot product I use is used to work out the angle between two vectors. Using a and b again,

a.b = |a|*|b|*cos(x) where x is the angle between the two vectors.

a.b = (5*2) + (6*3) (multiply the i values and the j values and add them together)

|a| = square root of (5^2 + 6^2) (think pythagorus: |a| means the size of a

using these, find out what cosx is, find out what x is.

from your quote,

Quote
a negative dot product means that a and b point away from each other; a positive dot product means they point in the same direction.

this makes sense: if x is > 180 degrees (they point away from each other) cosx will be negative, the same with x < 180 = cosx is positive.

edit: Phew. I think thats all correct, but anyone else feel free to put me in my place. Hope this helps, iangb

Maybe maths has a use after all!

also, about the user level replay thing, there is a slight issue. when i replay is put into the box when you beat the level, it gives you the data but can only be replayed if you have the level in your user level data.

$level Name#author#comments#mapdata#demodata#

This means that anything can be replayed. It's a good system.

#71736 16 2005-06-02T11:52:10Z iangb
ThWuMpA: when posting a level, can you pleeeeese post it in a text file, rather than just as a straight code dump, or it will be destroyed by the dreaded WordWrap. Both of the levels have errors in them, (NaNs), and just... *shudder*.

So.
1) get an account at NUMA. Put your maps there. If you post them here, put them in text files and attach them.
2) look at the site that is repeatedly linked to above. It's quite good.

As for the DDA, the error is probably caused by a NaN on one of your jump pads. Try to delete the pad that N hits and makes it 'float', and then replace it.
You normally get NaNs after pasting level data into the textbox and then pressing l to load the level, without clicking outside of the text box first. Don't do that, either.

I think thats all...

#72730 22 2005-06-06T08:10:47Z iangb
... resurrected due to me reading the new topic and following nevermore's advice....

Surely if you want to travel backwards in time, first you would need to make some method of instantanious transportation. (Like trekky teleporters, only instantanious). This is because otherwise, at the moment wher you stop going forwards in time and start to go backwards, your body (from 'going forwards') has to share the same space with your body (from 'going forwards'). That could be messy, unless when you were at 'null time' (stationary, neither forwards nor back) you could instantaniously be moved somewhere else, so you don't get 2 bodies in the same space. And technically, if nothing can go faster than the speed of light, then telportation is not possible either.

That is an interesting off-topic thing, actually. If nothing can go faster than the speed of light (including information) then if you had a really long pole, and you pulled one end towards you, the other end of the pole would not start moving until light could have gone from one end to the other.
Actually I think that scientists are just starting to think that information can be sent faster than the speed of light, because of quantum entanglement, whereby you have two fundamental particles, and when you do something to one of them, both are affected at the same time. In theory, this should happen even when separated by huge distances.

Oh, and Suki, I think that Daddaluma meant that you can go faster than the speed of light if you somehow accelerate so fast that you never actually hit the speed of light, instead you jump to a speed above it.
Which is also impossible, but there you go.

And speaking of applications... here's mine.

I'm 18, and I try to be the responsible 18-year-old, rather than the drunken/rowdy/irritating 18-year-old. I'm quite intelligent, in a maths/science sort of way (I'm off to study physics at university next year), and I enjoy using my mind.
I've been with the forum for over half a year now, and I think I've made sense for most of my time here. I'm quite all-round empathic - I try to see everybody's point of view, including my own, but I'm not afraid to stick up for my own point of view if I am the only one with that view. I don't like spamming/trolling/flaming - in general I'm a peacefull kinda guy.
I was one of the first members of Tsukatu's religious debating forums, and I (relatively) regularly take part in debates at various other forums, but I have never befor been in a position of power in a forum before. I do learn fast however - I could get to grips with new tools quickly.

I love N, think it's a great game, and have made some innovative maps in my time aswell (see my sig). I'm no highscores ubermaster, but I enjoy playing what is the main reason for this community to exist.

Out in the real world, I have had quite a bit of responsibility helping to run a scout troop, so I know how to deal with irritating young'uns without being too heavy-handed. I lead a relatively busy life, doing piano and climbing and reading and stuff, but I go onto the forums whenever I can - I don't have 'regular hours', but I'll be online five or six days out of seven. And in a British timezone, so I can be modding while LV/Keron are getting their beauty sleep.

Cons (just for you, Keron):
I can get irritated over small, unimportant things, although I can normally back off and calm down quite fast. My spelling/grammer isn't perfect, and I guess I am sometimes not serious enough - I tend to try and look on the bright/funny side.
I honestly don't think I have many other major deficiencies that would get in the way of being a mod (that probably makes me sound bigheaded, but I think it's pretty true).

I think that I could keep newbies in line without scaring them off, and without irritating other forum members. What do you think?

Edited repeatedly to include some cons aswell as pros, and because I thought of some more stuff to say...

#76978 11 2005-06-21T10:33:53Z iangb
2 things.

1) JeR(K) - you took your map data without resetting your map. The ninja should start on top of the bounce block, right?
So everyone else - put the ninja one square above the bounce block (go into edit mode)before playing the demo. Unless JeR(K) fixes the map data.

2) I think that it is because the floorguard algorithm checks every tile that the floorguard can go to, to see if the ninja is there (if it is there, then the floorguard moves as far as possible in that direction). As at the end of the demo, the ninja is on the same tile as the one the floorguard is on, so it is not detected, because the floorguard doesn't check it's own tile (programming that adjustment in would be possible, but I can see why M&R thought there was no need in the first place). If, at the end of the demo, you move a little bit to the left, onto the other tile, then the floorguard reacts.

Solved!

#77231 9 2005-06-22T08:40:56Z iangb
I don't know how much (physical, biological) evolution now applies to humanity now. The old story for evolution is that a single mutation gets passed on because that mutation makes the carrier more likely to survive, and breed. But with the rise of intelligence, the theory is no longer as applicable because everyone has a very high chance of survival anyway, so any special 'talant' is more likely to be ignored. Or worse, considered abnormal, and therefore removed from the gene pool.
What evolves now in humanity is culture. Political ideas, and the way we live are changing wi the generations, adapting to new circumstances. Communism was a social 'mutation' - one that was sucessfull and prospered for a short while. Now multiculturalism and global communication are becoming more 'acceptable', as attitudes adapt to the fact that if we constantly hate all other humans then the end result will be all-out war.

Anyway, on-topic. I think that for quite a lot of the population, that is true. They go through life with closed eyes and minds, never properly thinking about things, following the leader and believing what they are told. But for the people who do think for themselves - that is an evolving idea, a sign that society is slowly changing.

As for aliens - no, the universe is not infinite. It is a (roughly) spherical body, and outside it is... nothing. Not a big space filled with vacuum (*shudder* at those last three words, physicists), but nothing No space, no time. So really, there is no 'outside' the universe - yes the universe is expanding, but it is not expanding into anything. But the universe today is very, very, very big. Even bigger than that. So yes, I reckon that there are other life forms out there. We might not see them for a while - if a planet is on the other side of the universe (and we could somehow see it, which is a small problem) then the light we see from it today is light that came from that planet hundreds of millions of years ago. How much life was there on earth back then?

Accelerate as much as possible. But use the X cannon to slow yourself down if you have too many bullets coming at you, and remember that each enemy bullet you shoot with the X cannon gives you points, which (when you get enough) means that you get another 15 seconds bonus time.

Strafe as much as possible - the triangular bullets all aim for where you will be if you don't move sideways at all, so if you strafe lots then you will almost never be hit by one of them.

I think that that's it...

Quote: maximo, 2005-07-13T10:02:03Z
why does the saying "there is a first time for everything" exist when something like this:

Quote
You being ransacked by a moroding horde of blood thirsty pink unicorns hell bent on bringing an end to violence in the world via the use of excessive fear to scare the mean out of everyone... all wearing skirts with white lacing and their names handstiched on my a naked midget clown wearing clothes for the first time in his life.

isn't ever gonna have a first time?
In an infinite universe, anything that is physically possible can - and will - happen. If you flip coins for eternity, you are guarenteed (sp?) to get 1000 heads in a row at some point - in fact you should get that outcome an infinitely large number of times. The human mind is very bad at encompasing just what exactly infinity is. We tend to think of it as just a very very big number, forgetting that and number can have 1 added to it. So if the universe goes on for infinity, and the situation you described is physically possible, then it will happen for the first time. And probably for many times after that. I don't know how physically possible bloodthirsty pink unicorns are, though.

And evolution, like any scientific theory, can be disproven if there is enough evidence against it. The trouble is that there isn't any evidence against it (that I know of - and I think I missed out on the first Evolution debate). Much like the beliefs of an atheist, or a Catholic, can be disproven - but we are unlikely to get any evidence for either side. The only thing we can do is to interpret the facts we do have in our own ways - leading to differing beliefs across the world.

#84459 29 2005-07-18T21:08:35Z iangb
... I don't think I can add much to what's allready been said. I got to this thread too late.

The only new thing I can think of is the probability that neither Her nor M are the 'right' one for you. So if either does as before ('I really like you, but as a friend') be grateful for their friendship, and try to treat them as any normal friend - don't worry about 'scaring them off' in a way that would not affect a normal friend of yours. (And if you do somehow distance yourself from them by acting as yourself, then any romantic relationship would probably have been doomed from the start - someone should love you for what you are rather than what you are pretending to be.) It's hard, but you have to try and remember that you are not the only person who is 'trying to see what the other person is thinking'. If you are merely polite and formal with someone then they can take it the wrong way and start acting the same way, when neither of you are being truly honest - to yourselves aswell as to each other.

I had a similar - vaguely - situation about a year and a half ago - I asked out a girl who I had know since year 8-and-a-half who was clever, charming, funny - you name it, she had it. I got the same reply - 'friends only'. And I - subconciousley - slammed up barriers between us. We still talked, but not even as friends really, more as classmates. Slowly things returned to friendship again. About a term after I asked her out she started going out with a guy who is one of my good friends. I didn't have any real problem with that, but again I somehow found myself drifting away in friendship - oddly, only with the girl, not with the guy. But I sat down, gave myself a mental kick up the arse and went into school one week open and friendly, and we are now still great friends - just great friends, but I'm content with that.
The irritating thing now is that this whole episode was possibly only in my head - I don't know if anyone else (girl included) noticed a difference in me or not. But it doesn't matter - it's happened now and I am just carrying on as normal.

Anyway, what I'm trying to say is - be yourself, be friendly, but don't be heartbroken if all fails.

I also agree with maximo - if you love someone you should be thinking of them before you. But you do have to be able to think for yourself aswell. The tricky bit is finding a balance.

I hope some of the above makes sense. Good luck!

#91996 5 2005-08-17T20:23:35Z iangb
Three (and a half) counters to your counter.

0.5.) We got lucky. Get over it.

1.) The anthropic principle bit. If the universe had been unable to support life then we would not have been here to observe it and say 'this proves that humanity exists (or not) on the whim of God'.

2.) If there is a chance that humanity will exist given a certain set of circumstances and a universe does not have those circumstances, then no matter, just wait until the next big bang (as gravity eventually pulls everything back together) and hope you get a better set of circumstances. You may have to wait a few million million (repeated millions of times) centuries, but as there is no living creatur to observe it, the time doesnt matter. Time does not exist for you when you sleep. Eventually the circumstances will be correct. If there is a chance an event will happen, no matter how small that chance, in an infinite length of time that event is certain to happen (in fact, if the chance remains a constant then it will happen an infinite number of times. If you throw a dice for infinity then you will get 1000 sixes in a row eventually.

3.)The 'Life needs these circumstances to be created' story is a load of rubbish. Sure, humanity may have existed only under a certain set of conditions, but we do not know what would have happened in a different set of circumstances. A good analogy here is yourself. Imagine all the different possible DNA combinations you could have had given your parents (eg loads - a couple could have many many children, and none of them would be the same). Now imagine all the choices you have made, from what subjects you take to what colour pants you wear each day. The chance that you will have made those exact choices, will have had that exact DNA is minute, hugely small. Even more if you factor in the DAN of your parents, and of their parents, etc... But you still exist. And if you had made many of those choices differently, you (or a varied 'type' of you) would currently exist (admittedly dead if you made some really bad choices). It's like throwing a many-sided dice - there is a tiny chance that each side will come up, but it a certainty that one will. And we do not know how many 'sides' the dice of the universe has, and how many lead to humanity, or how many lead to other forms of life, or how many lead to nothing but the cold and the dark.

4.)(I know, I said I would give 3 important points, but this is related). There have been experiments using really powerful computers to try and model the big bang, and to show the outcome of changing the initial conditions of the early universe, and these have 'shown' that there are mant potential universes where, for example, carbon could not have been created, so life could also not have been created. But these experiments are flawed for several reasons. Firstly, even with all the computers in the world today you could not even model the behaviour of 12g of carbon - ~6*10^23 atoms. There simply isnt enough memory in the computeres to 'remember' each particle, even if you made each one represented by a single byte (8 ones or noughts). Secondly, even in those conditions life might still have appeared. Thirdly, and most importantly, the scientists assumed that each of the initial condition of the univers was unconnected, that you could change gravity without affecting magnetism. This is like marvelling that no matter where you touch a live wire you get a shock. So don't belive them.

I think that's all....
#92285 141 2005-08-18T22:19:37Z iangb
Quote: maximo, 2005-08-18T21:14:34Z
If I have infinite marbles and give you half of them; infinity/2=infinity
Your maths isn't quite right. Infinity is not a number. It is a concept that can be used in maths, but not in the same way that normal numbers can (like imaginary number i). So for the 'infinity' numbers system, it is completely possible for half of infinity to equal infinity, because you cannot treat infinity as a normal number.

roughly, infinity * x = infinity, unless x = 0, in which case infinity * 0 = 0. As division is simply multiplying by 1/x the same is true for that. Adding anything other than -infinity to infinity = infinity, but infinity - infinity = 0.
You cannot have half an infinite number of marbles.

If there is a finite chance something will happen then in an infinite universe it is guarenteed to happen. There is no such thing as an infinite chance - if something is non-zero then it is finite, no matter how small it is (for a chance ranging from 0 to 1).

The real question therefore is - is an event physically possible. If it is, then there is a finite - maybe very very small, but still finite - chance that it will happen, so in an infinte universe it is guaranteed to happen. If it is not physically possible then the chance of it happening is 0 - and so it will never happen. Ever. Not in this universe, anyway.

I don't really have a point to this post, but it explains some stuff at least.

As far as I can tell, you are saying that by putting a metal object (warm) into a freezer, you cause the refrigerant to lose energy, and therefore freeze. One of the laws of thermodynamics is that a body does not pass energy to somewhere which allready has greater energy. IE - hot things get colder when surrounded by cold things, while the cold things warm up a little. So there is no way that the refrigerant can freeze because you put something metal in your fridge.

#108904 11 2005-10-17T11:03:49Z iangb
Very good.

Kinda long-winded, and made vulgar for the sake of appealing to the masses (of browsers of pointlesswasteoftime, that is) but good.

But there a few half-decent answers from the 'free will' point of view of things.

1. There is no absolute equation to predict the way things (on Heisenburg's small scale) will happen - you can only predict the chance that things will happen. Schrodingers Cat is a good example of this - you cannot tell whether the cat is alive or dead, only the probability that the cat is either alive or dead. At the quantum scale, matter is not predictable.

2. It is (as the Heisenburg Uncertainty Principle states) impossible to know the exact position and velocity of any subatomic particle. And this is not just because the photons 'bounce off' the particles and affect it - if you could (somehow) put an electron in a box, and then slowly make the box shrink (therefore narrowing the places where the electron could be - and therefore making you know where it is more accurately), the electron will move faster and change direction at random - unpredictably.

I have a less scientific point of view aswell, but I can't sort out what I want to say. Basically, yes, emotions are a human concept. But you can only react to the univerce that you perceive, and if the universe you perceive contains those concepts then you must (and we all do) treat those concepts as real.

Finally, an afterthought. Who said that 'Mind' has to be material? If it is immaterial then it is not bound by a physical law and can then be unpredictable. The same concept applies to 'Soul', allthough I see that as a mind that has caught relligion.

Maybe a totally unconnected and isolated observer could predict the future of something else, but as soon as the observer/calculator becomes involved in their own calculations then it all breaks down.

So basically, the universe may be predictable to an isolated observer who cannot influence the universe in any way (so not God then, as He (if He exists) influences the universe), but as we are all contained within the universe it is impossible for us to predict it.

Quote: Jesse, 2005-10-22T13:48:27Z
The universe is finite, but you can't reach the edge of it. Just like there's no edge of the Earth. You can go in a straight line and eventually you'll end up where you started. Space is like that, only in 3 dimensions (length width depth) instead of 2 dimensions (length width)
That's what I thought was a good explanation too - and there are lots of recent theories about it. But now I'm not so sure...

Let me deviate a little, into the strange realm of special relativity. One of the eqations of special relativity states that time slows down for someone who is moving relative to the observer. This has been proven - atomic clocks have been set to the same time, then one has been flown around the world in a jet. When reunited, the one that went around the world was a few nanoseconds behind the one that was stationary.
Now this confused a lot of physicists, because of the 'Twin Paradox'. Say we have a pair of twins, imaginatively called A and B. They are both in empty space, with A's velocity relative to B as 0.9 times the speed of light. A then reverses direction, and returns to B at the same speed. When the twins meet again, the physicists saw a problem. From Bs point of view, A went away and returned and so should have aged less, because A was moving very fast. However, from As point of view it is B that has gone away and come back, so B should have aged less. Obviously they cannot both be younger that the other one. So there is a bit of a paradox, which spelt bad news for the theory.
This paradox was solved by the fact that one of the twins has to experience acceleration to change direction, so special relativity can no longer apply to that twins point of view - it is the one who will have aged less.

Anyway, back to the main problem. If the universe is circular (you can go in a straight line and return to your start point) then twin A could leave and return to twin B without either twin experiencing acceleration, so the paradox re-appears. A tricky problem.

Any comments on that little bit of randomness?

#110083 355 2005-10-23T23:43:16Z iangb
Quote: nevermore, 2005-10-23T15:13:19Z
String theory... I've heard quite a bit about it, and I must admit I don't understand it at all. Are you an expert on the matter? I'd really appreciate a real explanation of it.
I'm no expert, but I'm starting my physics degree at uni this year, and on of the books we had to read was called The Elegant Universe, by Brian Greene, which was basically all about string theory. I definitely reccomend it.

String theory was created to solve the fundamental problem in modern physics - that General relativity and Quantum Mechanics do not both work together. Normally this is not a problem, because General Relativity (GR) is for big/heavy things, whereas Quantum Mechanics (QM) is for small, lightweight things. But for certain cases, such as for black holes, neither theory works properly. This is because GR assumes that the fabric of spacetime is more or less uniform. Gravity bends spacetime, and so on. QM however says that at a small scale the fabric of spacetime is a 'quantum froth' - a constantly changing, wildly unpredictable... froth.
String theory solves the problem by saying that instead of fundamental substances and forces being made of point-particles, they are instead made of strings that vibrate in different ways, giving each string properties such as mass and charge. The clever bit is that a string is too large to be affected by the 'quantum froth', so the extra problems can be safely ignored.

There is a lot more complications (such as the theory predicts 11 dimensions, with the extra ones 'curled up' so they cannot be detected), but that is the basic theory.

Then there are lots of interesting inferences from the theory that explain many unanswered questions - why gravity is a much weaker force than the other three, and a bit about the big bang and why we live in a three (plus time) dimensional universe. So yeah, it's all fun.

#114581 8 2005-11-13T17:30:13Z iangb
Quote: nevermore, 2005-11-13T05:18:19Z
... if theoretically we were able to accelerate to a speed faster than the speed of light, we would be moving backwards in time.
I'm not sure that's true.

The equation for time dilation is T (time measured by observer)=To(time measured by moving person)/(square root of (1-(u^2)/(c^2)))

If u (speed of moving person) = c (the speed of light) then time will stop for the moving person. But if u>c then the equation requires the square root of a negative number, which does not (physically, at least) exist.

Tricky.

YOU KNOW YOU'VE BEEN IN UNIVERSITY TOO LONG WHEN...

*Parents' cooking becomes something you desire, not avoid.
*You schedule your classes around sleep habits and soap operas,
especially neighbours and Murder She Wrote.
*You know the pizza boy by name and don't even need to read the menu.
*You go to sleep when it's light and get up when it's dark.
*You live for getting mail.
*Looking out the window is a form of entertainment.
*Prank  phone calls become funny again.
*You start thinking and sounding like your friends and your accent
becomes a hybrid of West Country, Surrey and general Northern.
*Highlighters are the coolest things on earth.
*Rearranging your room is your favourite pastime.
*Rubbish cheap £1 shops are so cool.
*The weekend lasts from Thursday to Monday.

BEFORE I CAME TO UNIVERSITY, I WISH I HAD KNOWN...

*That it didn't matter what my first lecture was, I'd still sleep through it.
*That I could change so much and barely realize it.
*That you can love a lot of people in a lot of different ways.
*No matter how 'cool' you were in school, no one here cares.
*That if you wear polyester everyone will ask why you are so dressed  up.
*That every clock on campus shows a different time.
*That if you got good a-levels, so what? It doesn't matter here.
*That I would go to a party the night before an exam or essay due-date.
*That you can know everything and fail a test.
*That you can know nothing and ace a test.
*That I could get used to almost anything found out about my friends.

*That friendship is more than getting drunk together but that's still funny!
*That Sunday is a figment of the world's imagination.
*That Psychology is really Biology, that Biology is really Chemistry,
that Chemistry is really Physics and that Physics is really Maths.
*That my parents would become so much smarter in the last few  years.
*That it's possible to be alone even when you are surrounded by friends.
*Don't be dismayed at good-byes, a farewell is necessary before we can
meet again, and meeting again, after moments or a lifetime, is certain
for those who are friends.

TOP 10 REASONS THAT UNIVERSITY IS LIKE PRIMARY SCHOOL:

10. You cry for your mummy.
9. You cross the street without looking for cars.
8. Snack time is a necessity.
7. You bundle up for the outdoors without caring what you look like
(because everyone else looks as stupid as you do).
6. You stay at home and play games with your friends.
5. You wear your backpack on both shoulders.
4. You wear big mittens.
3. Playing in the snow is a legitimate activity.
2. You take naps.
1. You look forward to cheese toasties.

you can't really 'save' a level in-game, as such. Instead just copy the data from the top textbox of Ned into a notepad file, and save the file. To load your level again, paste that data back into the top box, CLICK ON THE MAIN WINDOW (not in a textbox, or when you load the level you will type an L in the level data, corrupting it), and hit L. That will re-load the level for playing.

S in Ned doesn't save the game to disk - it just copies the data to the Clipboard so from there it's a simple matter of ofening notepad and selecting 'Paste'.

#133183 72 2006-01-17T16:23:20Z iangb
radio waves and gamme waves travel at pretty much the same speed, in air. In a vacuum, they travel at identical speeds.

Oh, and the black holes thing is nearly true: It relys on there being an 'opposite' of black holes, called white holes. Anything that you put in the black hole comes out from the white hole.
Take the white hole, and accelerate it to near-lightspeed. After a 30 years, you have a black hole which is 30 years old, and a white hole that is (say) only 3 years old (since date of discovery). Put an object in the black hole, and it should come out of he white hole, 27 years earlier. Voila!
The only problem is: white holes may well not exist, and 'linking' one too a black hole is quite a tricky prospect, if at all possible

Much easier is to travel forwards in time: accelerate yourself to relativistic velocities and it'll take you a few minutes to jump years into the future. The only propblem with that idea (on a large scale, at least), is that it's physically very hard to accelerate anything to near-lightspeed. And once you've gone to the future, you can't come back.

Oh, and on the subject of the speed of light:
Yes, if you are travelling at the speed of light, time will not pass for you (allthough I'm not sure you'd want to be instantly at the end of time, if such a thing exists). But you can't accelerate to the speed of light, because your mass increases as you go faster, so you need more and more force for a dwindlingly small amount of acceleration. And going faster than the speed of light does not guarentee going backwards in time (once you've got past the problem of having infinte mass). The equation basically breaks if you go faster: it starts to involve the square root of a negative number, which is imaginary.

(yes, I've said some of this a page or so ago. Well, it's your fault for not reading the earlier posts).

the problem is... at the moment, the replays are done based on the fabulousness of the physics system: all that are recorded are the keypresses, and the game engine does the rest. It's determinism in action (a certain set of actions allways lead to the same result).

If you were to do a 'ghost run', then things such as the position of bounce blocks would affect the run. Plus doors, etc...

So M&R would have to find a new way of 'recording' map runs, which is a pretty hard thing to do.

#135738 4 2006-01-25T16:07:38Z iangb
Nope. Google gives each website a score based on how many sites link to that website, weighed by the 'popularity' of each of those sites.

Word-wise, it looks for sites containing the word and sites that are linked to with the link as that word. So linking to NUMA like this: cheese! would give google a hit whenever someone searched for 'Cheese!', even though the site itself doesn't contain that word.

Big companies can pay to appear as 'sponsered links', and I think it costs the depending on the popularity of the word they want to be associated with. Eg "sport" or "bank" costs a lot more than "toenail".

#135962 15 2006-01-26T01:38:03Z iangb
Nothing is certain. Nothing. Mainly because of:

For an event to be certain, it has to be predicted.
Once an event has been predicted, it can be changed. In fact, the very act of prediction may change the event.

Therefore, nothing is absolutely certain. However, many things are pretty guarenteed. Like: if I let go of an object with mass, it will fall towards nearest strongest centre of gravity. Or F=MA.

Quote: BSBen, 2006-01-30T23:00:04Z
How do you get a .sol file to save somewhere other than where it is supposed to be without it being corrupted? I need to back up my files.
Just:
Play N.
Go into the folder containing the .sol file (C:\Documents and Settings\[your user name]\Application Data\Macromedia\Flash Player\#SharedObjects\[random letters/numbers]\localhost)
Copy the file n_v14b_userdata.sol to somewhere else.

Done!

To restore your data, simply copy the .sol file back into the main folder.

#139931 20 2006-02-05T20:43:51Z iangb
...no.

You've managed to delete your .sol file (basically the .sol file is the N save file). Clearing cookies will _not_ do this. A bug in the game sometimes does - unfortunately there isn't anything you can do about it. Next time, back up your .sol file periodically by copying it out of it's folder to somewhere else.

The .sol file is stored in this folder: C:\Documents and Settings\[your user name]\Application Data\Macromedia\Flash Player\#SharedObjects\[random set of letters/numbers]\localhost


edit: oh, and don't use cheats to try and get back to where you were - it means you won't be able to unlock any secrets.

#6713 1 2006-02-07T20:30:58Z iangb
Well, you know what this means. The game is basically the same as last time, with a new and improved set of Judges - me, Atilla, Sweep and Red Reamer. There are small changes - see below - but the main idea remains the same. (Incidentally, the last scavenger hunt took place here)

The Rules -
We (iangb, Sweep, Red Reamer and Atilla) will continue to post as normal throughout the forum and NUMA. However, in some of our posts we will include referances. Each judge will post a maximum of 25 referances, 5 from each category: Literature, Film/TV, Games, Music and Misc. Misc can be anything that doesn't fall into any of the other categories, or it can be and extra referance from a 'full' category (like a sixth 'Music' referance, or similar).

The aim of the game for you, the players, is to find as many referances as possible. Ideally, we will have made 100 referances between us, allthough this isn't guarenteed to happen. When you find a referance, PM the author with the referance and where it is from to get a point.

Surprisingly enough, the person with the most points wins.

The judges can start posting referances whenever they wish, but they will post here to let you know when they are going to start. This slightly more staggered start will (hopefully) keep your interest without making it impossible to start playing a bit later on (like, in a few days time if you miss the topic first time around).

So there we go. Post here if you have any questions/comments, and keep an eye out for referances! A 'standings' topic will also be made, once some people have got points.

EDIT: I have been told (thanks, Dadd) that I keep spelling reference wrong. Oh well...

Yup. For what it's worth, I am 100% in agreement with Tsukatu. Hell, I'd be a Satanist if I wasn't content with my current way of living.

I went to church twice over Christmas. Once for a Christmas event, once for a funeral. They had very different effects on me.
The funeral made me angry at the church. My grandfather had died, and here was this man telling me that, as long as I believed in God, he would be in heaven? It seemed to me that it was nothing but false hope - when someone dies you should celebrate their life, not say 'horray he's in a better place now'. We don't know that, either way. I'd prefer to live my life to the fullest, rather than hope that I go somewhere better after death.
The christmas sermon made me slightly envious. The supportive, all-loving Church is a great thing to belong to. It brings security, calm, and knowledge that no matter what happens - you have friends. If you truly believed, then that would be a fantastic thing to live with. But I somehow cannot accept the facts that go with the belief - the parts that involve ritual, and a belief in a self-contradictory book and what it says. So I choose the middle path. I live well according to what I see as 'living well'. If I'm right then that's great, if I'm wrong then I am just as wrong as the Church. My principles are what I live by, and those are ... (continued in another thread, if I ever get around to it).

(I realise this may have degenerated into a rant. Sorry.)

Hah, you're getting the whole 'awkward silence' thing. Yeah, that happens, and I've gone through it a couple of times(under slightly different circumstances). The only thing to do is: be patient. Keep on being friendly, don't give up.

I think (note: my opinion only) that people have a kind of 'mental image' about everyone they know, and that image can take a while to change. For example, I allways used to be the shortest out of a group of people and I still kept the 'midget' nickname for a while after I was taller than most of them. But over time that image of me as 'the short kid' was replaced by the image of 'me as I am now, the immensly cool guy([/sarc])'. I think you get a certain type of behaviour associated with the mental image - "that's how I react towards him", basically. And that, too, takes a while to change. But it will.

As for your wierd girl... I don't know her, so I can't say exactly what to do. But I would reccomend reviewing your own 'mental picture' of her. She's probably not as bad as you think she is.

*** INSTRUCTIONS ****************************************************************************

This file contains data used to fill the [User Levels] menu in N;
editing the contents of this file allows you to alter the contents of the in-game menu.
We recommend that you turn Word Wrap off to edit this file.


It's _very_ important that you format data properly when adding it to this file,
or who knows what will happen. Wait, I know: something bad.


To add a level to the list, simply add it into this file using the following syntax:

$levelname#authorname#comments#leveldata#

(it's _very_ important that you don't forget the final "#" after the level data!!)

The fields should be self-explanitory:
levelname: the name of the level, i.e "superliminal"
authorname: the name of the person who made the level, i.e "jimmy"
comments: you can use this field to describe the level type, i.e "easy", "hard", "boring", etc.
leveldata: data describing the level, usually taken from the level editor


Level and author names which contain "#" will produce errors.
You can add text between level data as long as it doesn't contain "$" or "#" characters. This is helpful
for separating levels within this file, as you can see below.


If you're a bit confused, please browse the included level data; it will hopefully provide you
with some insight as to what needs to be done in order to add/remove user levels.

Obviously, renaming or moving this file will result in problems.
You're welcome.

Quote: AV_Ultima, 2006-02-25T17:09:39Z
Let me get this straight:

1)Go to numa copy map data.
2)Go to ned(~) paste in top box.
3)Find comment to that same map with demo data and copy it.
4)Go back to ned(~) and paste that in bottom box.

Not quite. You missed a few important bits.

EITHER (Ned)
1)Go to numa copy map data.
2)Go to ned(~) paste in top box.
2.5) CLICK OUTSIDE THE BOX, then press L
3)Find comment to that same map with demo data and copy it.
4)Go back to ned and paste that in bottom box.
5)CLICK OUTSIDE THE BOX, make sure caps lock is ON
6)Press 3, then Q, then P.

OR (Userlevels)

1) Go to NUMA, copy '1.4+ map data'
2)In N, go to the userlevels menu. Paste the userlevels data in the textbox.
3)In NUMA, copy the appropriate demo data
4)In N, paste the demo data into the same textbox, immediately after the '1.4+ map data'. Add a # to the end of it all
5)Click the 'watch replay' button.

Ian's Student Snack (1)

Ingredients: Oil, Bread, 2 Eggs, Cheese (Red Leicester for preferance)

Put a small amount of oil in a frying pan and put a slice of bread in on top of it. Pour a bit more oil over the top (the bread shouldn't be dripping, but a decent amount of oil is good) and turn on the heat so the bread is nicely fried (looks like pale toast, and has just aquired the crispy texture on the outside. If the oil is hot it shouldn't take long) Careful when turning the bread - hot oil hurts if it lands on you (voice of experience).
Put the bread on a plate, and using the remaining oil (add a bit more if you need to) fry your two eggs in whatever style you want, 'though personally I like sunny side up. Put the fried eggs on your fried bread.
Finally, grate as much cheese over it as you feel is necessary.

Consume. Feel your arteries clang shut with the pure greasyness of it all. Enjoy.

(short version: fry bread, fry eggs, grate cheese, eat)

#151118 57 2006-03-03T14:15:31Z iangb
On that point of view...: if the future is totally predictable and set out, there is no way of predicting it. Because if you could predict the future then you could inflence it so that your prediction was incorrect.
The only way you could predict the future was if you were 100% seperate from the thing you were predicting (ie observing but not affecting).
Unfortunately, on a sub-atomic level (according to Heisenburg's Uncertainty Principle) the very act of observing something affects it, so ultimately the future cannot be predicted on a subatomic level. As chaos theory nicely states, very tiny changes can have massive outcomes, so those sub-atomic differences can eventually result in a macroscopic (ie real-world) change. So ultimately, the future is not predictable to any great certainty, and that certainty decreaces further with time, and size (of the system that is being predicted).

I therefore state that free will does exist, or at least that if free will doesn't exist then we have no way of proving it. Fin.

EDIT: oh, and Solarion: The universe will never cool to absolute zero. It may get very close, but no point in the universe will ever get to 0K. I'm just being nitpicky.

#151505 67 2006-03-04T13:38:01Z iangb
This, Tsukatu, is what I have a problem with.

Quote: Tsukatu, 2006-03-04T07:02:20Z
the notion that all forms of matter will have one outcome and one outcome only.

We have ablolutely no proof that this is so. The fact that everything we view on a macroscopic scale is nice and predictable is totally different to the 'quantum froth' you get when going down to tiny tiny tiny tiny tiny tiny tiny tiny tiny tiny tiny tiny tiny tiny tiny tiny tiny tiny tiny tiny tiny tiny tiny tiny tiny tiny tiny tiny tiny tiny tiny tiny scale, where spacetime looks more like, well, froth on top of a pan of boiling water, and a lot less predictable. It's that that's giving classical theoretical physicists multiple headaches. The idea of a 'clockwork universe' may well be a totally false one.

Or, alternately, the universe may be absolutely deterministic and free will does not exist. But until that is proven (unlikely, due to my paradox as above), I would say that free will exists.

Heh, you could say that free will exists in the same way that emotion exists. It's there and we see it's effects every day, but it is a human construct. Whether you take that in a deterministic way or a metaphysical way is up to you.

#151599 16 2006-03-04T19:50:31Z iangb
@Evil:That's sort of what I meant. If you've ever played around with UnrealEd, you'll understand it a bit more.

In that, the bot's pathfinding works thusly: In the map is an invisible network of 'nodes', linked together. The bot's 'midn' cycle works something like this:
1)Find where the bot is, and the status of the bot, and the positions/distances (via the node network) of all items.
2)Decide what the bot wants to do - ie get health, shoot a player, etc...
3)Using the network and a relatively simple algorithm, find the shortest route, going from node to node, between the bot and it's target node.
4)move bot along the path to the target node. This is the hard bit (with jumping calculations, etc),
5)redo from start.

With N the ninja can get to different places depending on it's speed, so the 'potential' network would be much, much harder to lay out.

Oh. My. God.

There's a free version-thingy of a Trackmania game! Right Here

For those of you who have never played this fantastic, fantastic game, it's basically to Gran Turismo what N is to Super Mario Brothers. In fact, there are many similarities between trackmania and N.
Both have fantastic physics engines, both are tile-based. The original trackmania had a puzzle element in it - you had to set up the tiles so the track was as fast as possible. Or, you could just race. And you had to use the physics to race well - breaking before a down slope so you get a perfect landing off it at the end, etc...

Really, Trackmania is one of my favouritest games ever. And they've released a free stand-alone addon! Excellent!

Quote: Twistkill, 2006-03-19T02:05:16Z
Evolution is, in my opinion, wrong. Here's why I believe so:

Why does the evolution theory say we evolved from monkeys? If we did, why do monkeys still exist today? Surely they would have all evolved, right? What's also strange is spontaneous generation. How can a living thing come from something with no organic make-up whatsoever?

Scientists are finding insects fossilized in amber. Sometimes, the same species is found living today. Surely, according to evolution, the organism would have evolved and changed to something different, right? This goes in accordance with my monkey statement above.

What do people have to say about my post?
Paragraph the first: We did not evolve from monkeys. Nor did we evolve from any other species currently on Earth. Yes, we probably shared a common ancestor, but since then the species have become different: evolved into two seperate species, both of which were best suited for their particular environment.

Paragraph the second:Evolution generally happens only when there is competition: mutations still occur, but none of those mutations give a difference between life and death, so that mutation is not passed on particlularly specially. Animals like alligators (and many insects) are perfectly suited for their environment, and have no real competitors, so they haven't evolved for millenia.

EDIT: I just saw the 'spontanious generation' thing. Answering...

Quote: Twistkill, 2006-03-19T02:05:16Z
How can a living thing come from something with no organic make-up whatsoever?
Well, for a start, there are many, many naturally occuring organic compounds (organic means pretty much any molecule with carbon in). Methane is probably the most common. To make more complex organic compounds, all you need is to combine the simple 'building blocks' - mainly organic molecules containing carbon, oxygen, nitrogen and hydrogen.
More complex molecules can then combine to form simple proteins, complex proteins, etc...

Running (and expanding a bit) with my earlier definition - free will is the ability to choose between possible outcomes. You may be influenced by external forces, but ultimately the choice is yours, for better or worse.

I think Tsukatu's point was this:

1)If an absolutely (ie one unconfined by not only the laws of physics, but the laws of logic) omnipotent deity exists , then it is all-knowing, meaning it can predict the future with 100% accuracy.
2)If the future can be predicted with 100% accuracy, then free will can not exist. The 'choices' we make are predetermined, predictable by physical (and metaphysical, if they exist) laws
3)Therefore if an absolutely omnipotent deity exists, then free will cannot. At least, human free will cannot exist - the deity will be the sole possesor of free will.

Therefore an ablolutely omnipotent God and the existence of human free will are mutually exclusive.

EDIT: @rse, I just thought of a loophole, so the whole argument falls through. If the deity is absolutely omnipotent, then it can will away the paradox. After all, it is unconstrained by logic.

It's a rubbish argument, but it nicely shows a different point. It is impossible to scientifically/logically disprove the existence of God. All the believers have to say is 'It doesn't matter. He is God', and their faith will lead them on. Equally, you cannot prove the existence of God - anything like that can be explained by the fact that we don't know everything about the way the universe works.

All that's left is whether you choose to believe in god or not. And if free will doesn't exist, you don't even have that - you just think you do. But I digress.

#158905 60 2006-03-28T17:20:09Z iangb
Yes, but it doesn't matter, because he is God.

Or you could choose to view it that way, at least. Paradoxes don't apply to something unconstrained by logic.

You are faced with a 3-way option.
1) God is absolutely omnipotent, in which case there is nothing that He cannot do - possible or impossible, by our standards. Just because we can't see (or even comprehend) how it happens doesn't mean it is impossible to a being of that power.

2) God is omnipotent, but is constrained by logic. So He couldn't make a rock that He couldn't lift, and He couldn't predict the future to 100% accuracy.

3) God does not exist.

In any of these three versions, the existence (or nonexistance) of free will plays no part. For 1 free will can exist because God is free from any logical paradoxes, for 2 it can exist because the future cannot be predicted and for 3 free will can exist because it feels like it.

Sorry.

Quote: Daddaluma, 2006-03-28T23:59:12Z
The argument above uses temporal terms like predict and future with regards to an omnipotent and omniscient being. But if we set God outside of time, then these words dont have any meaning and this argument gets really slippery. If God is outside of time, then he cant be said to be predicting our futures. All of our time is one big instant to him. All of our time happens in the same instant. All of the choices we make, and all of the results of those choices are all simultaneous to an extemporal God. So our future isnt determined. God only knows what happens because he is seeing what we will choose right now.
If God is outside time, and can see every instant in time simultaniously, then surely that is predetermination? God knows what we will choose because to Him, we have allready chosen it/are choosing it. That's not too different from God knowing what we will choose because He can predict it.
Ach, this is degenerating into semantics. My point is that if God knows what we -to us- will choose because -to God- we are choosing it, then that isn't free will, because we aren't choosing between two possible outcomes. Our future is predetermined, so there is only one possible outcome.

I really feel I could have worded that better.

Quote: tl0, 2006-04-03T19:46:35Z
after door 3 is opened, another person enters the room. for him/her, there are two doors with one treasure behind one of them. why hasn't he got a 50/50 chance?

That's explainable. Call the first person (who chose when there were 3 boxes) Alice. If a second person Bob enters the room after one of the boxes has been removed, then Bob will have a 50/50 chance of getting the right box. Alice, however, will have the improved chances. This is because the extra 3rd box has not been removed entirely at random: there has been interaction between Alice and the boxes (or at least the showman who removes the boxes) and this changes the probablity.

#166150 50 2006-04-18T13:24:30Z iangb
Heh, 7 minutes sounds about right to me.

iangb's top 16 songs over 7 minutes long

I limited myself to one song per band, or there would be many more Yes/Propellerheads songs in here. The only band I have missed out on is Pink Ffloyd, merely because I don't appear to have any of their longer songs on my laptop. My loss.

Not quite make-its (in no particular order): Jesus of Suburbia (Greenday), Calenders and Clocks (The Coral), Silverf*ck (The Smashing Pumpkins), Citizen Erased (Muse), Sway (lostprophets), First Circle (Pat Metheny), Smash (The Offspring) and quite a few others by Coldplay, Jimmy Eat World, Pendulum, Dragonforce and Idlewild, to name a few.



16.) The Stars Are Projecters, by Modest Mouse (8:46)
A trippy, lilting example of Modest Mouse's particular brand of genius. Dreamy, but sharp.

15.) Catherine Parr, by Rick Wakeman (7:55)
Flowing keyboard melodies from a member of Yes, this song sounds good and is aproximately impossible to play.

14.) Insomnia, by Faithless (8:41)
One of the ultimate dance tunes, I felt obliged to my student nature to include this one. Move to the beat.

13.) Freebird, by Lynard Skynard (9:07)
Better than 'Sweet Home Alabama', and just as styled. Takes some getting used to, but then you won't want to stop.

12.) Frozen, by Celldweller (7:00)
If you saw a trailer for the film Constantine a while ago, you will have heard a slight remix of this song. Rubbish lyrics, but a tune that you can't ignore.

11.) 21st Centuary Schitziod Man, by King Crimson (7:24)
Any song that includes the line "innocents raped with napalm fire" has to be good. Maybe. This is old, experimental, angry prog rock, and I love it.

10.) Crusader, by Chris De Burgh (8:47)
Old but not forgotten, this sounds fantasitic in spite of the slightly pretentious lyrics - and the fact that I recorded it off vinyl.

9.) Suppers Ready, by Genesis (24:33)
The cleverest lyrics in the list. And a fine, fine tune. A flower?

8.) Come Back, by the Foo Fighters (7:51)
This song varies between the melodic and the rocking, with a classic Foo guitar anthem supporting Dave Grohl's gravely voice. A song worthy of the Foo Fighters

7.) California One Youth and Beauty Brigade, by The Decemberists (9:50)
Inspiring a forum-wide conspiracy, this song sounds... unique. It champions the weak, and wins. Listen to the lyrics. Nothing will stand in our way.

6.) The Revealing Science of God, by Yes (20:26)
It's a Yes song. Need I say more? It has clever, flowing lyrics and creates, well, a topographic ocean of soundscape in your head. There were many many other potential Yes songs (Starship Trooper, The Gates Of Delerium, etc), but this was my favourite. It was a darn hard call, though.

5.) Art of Life, by X Japan (28:56)
There was no way I could miss this out. The longest song I know, it includes about 5 minutes of high-pitched fast-paced 'air guitar', followed by an equally long piano solo. The only reason it isn't higher is that the piano gets a little too experimental for my tastes.

4.) On Her Majesty's Secret Service, by The Propellerheads (9:20)
The classic James Bond theme, reworked with a beat. Like Clubbed to Death, you can just lean back, close your eyes, and listen.

3.) American Pie, by Don McLain (8:32)
Definitely Don's greatest piece (allthough others come close), this song is triumphant in its tragedy. Plus it has some of the most metaphorical lyrics there are.

2.) Clubbed To Death (Kurayamino Variation), by Rob Dougan (7:29)
The best chilled-out pure instrumental from Rob D, this song also includes the piano solo that is inspiring, soaring, and simple. The video for it ain't bad, either.

1.) Tubular Bells (Part 1) - Mike Oldfield (25:29)
This is probably one of the best know 'long songs' that there are. From the haunting initial melody that was used in The Excorcist to the triumphant finish ("Tubular Bells!"), this is a masterpiece.

#168702 58 2006-04-26T18:30:53Z iangb
Oh gawd...

It expands by all the stars moving further apart. We can tell that it's expanding because of doppler shift.

Doppler shift means that if a star/galaxy emits light while it is moving away from us, the wavelength we see is slightly longer than it should be, because the star is moving away from us. A similar, non-relativistic process applies to sound. Because we know what the light from the star/galaxy should look like (because elements making up a star always give out identical 'bands' of frequency, due to fixed energy levels of the electrons in the element), we can tell how fast the star is moving away relative to us.
We can also tell, by various methods that I can't remember right now (I am so going to fail my Astrology exam in a few weeks) how far away the star is from us. It turns out that the further away from us a star is, the faster it is moving away from us. You only get that effect if the entire universe is expanding. For a nice analogy of that, put some black dots on a white baloon, then blow the baloon up. As it expands, the dots will separate from each other in the same way.

Not true. Distance is quantised, just as energy is. Once you get down to the planck length (if an atom was the size of the universe then the planck length would be about the size of a tree) you cannot go any 'deeper'.

#179876 3 2006-05-24T18:00:36Z iangb
Stardeash, just because you haven't done it doesn't mean that it isn't possible.

It does happen sometimes. The only thing you can do about it is to back up your N save file periodically.
The save file is n_v14b_userdata.sol and is stored in the following folder (assuming you're running Windows XP):

C:\Documents and Settings\[your user name]\Application Data\Macromedia\Flash Player\#SharedObjects\[Random set of letters&numbers]\localhost

You will need to be able to view hidden files and folders to see it.

To back it up, just copy the .sol file to another folder (for example, the folder containing N). If your game gets reset, like has happened to you, just copy the file back into the original folder. Unfortuantely for you there is no way to recover lost data, but now at least you shouldn't have the same problem again.

Evolution, in a strictly biological sense, is when beneficial random mutations occur in an individual of a species, causing that individual to be better suited for survival and procreation in it's particular environment. Because that individual is 'better' at surviving, it is more likely that the next generation of the species will also contain the mutation.
Conversely, if the mutation is not beneficial, then the individual will not survive to pass on the mutation.

Originally, Pi was defined as C=2(Pi)R, where C = circumference of a circle and R=radius of the circle. From that simple equation, Pi=C/2R: so pi can be calculated by measuring the diameter and circumference of a circle very, very accurately and dividing one by the other. In that case, your precision of pi is limited by the accuracy of the measurements of the circle.

However, pi crops up unexpectedly in many places (for example, e^(Pi*i)=-1, which is very, very strange), so it wouldnt suprise me if there was an 'exact' value for pi.

All worldviews have a fundamental axiom, which cannot be proved.
Christianity's is that god exists, and is omnipotent.
Atheism's is that the universe behaves exactly as it is percieved: that logic is omnipotent
Agnosticism's is that nothing is certain (and we're not even sure about that)

For each different worldview, most of the rest of the worldview can be proven, but only using that fundamental axiom. If it is false then the whole worldview falls through.

That makes sense... but doesn't it work for integer numbers, aswell?

In non-integers, written numbers can go all the way to infinity (left-to-right), getting smaller as they go. If the number stops, then you can assume that the rest of the numbers are 0, all the way to infinity (for example, if the 6th decimal on tktktk's list was 0.0234 exactly then for his his calculated numbers he would have had to use 0.023400, giving .186370 and .297481.

But written integer numbers also go to infinity (right to left), getting larger as they go. So you can take your numbers from right to left.

eg:
0002354
0232678
6590786
8198719
0000012

to get 08774 and 19885

In other words: I'd say that there was more infinity than can be imagined, so all proofs relating to it are a little bit... odd. For example, this proof requires even just the the idea of an infinite list of numbers, which is impossible.

#9705 1 2006-06-26T09:41:01Z iangb
DISCLAIMER: THIS IS NOT A REAL PROOF. JUST SOMETHING TO INSPIRE YOU TO THINK A LITTLE

OK... proof that 1 = 2

First postulate: anything multiplied by 0 equals 0. So 0X=0 for all real values of X

Second postulate: doing the same things to both halves of an equation does not validate/invalidate the equation. So if A=B then AX=BX. Similarly, if A|=B (A is not equal to B) then AX|=BX (AX is not equal to BX).

let A = 1
let B = 2
let X = 0

Assume A=B <---thing to be proved

If A=B
Then AX=BX (by postulate 1)

As AX = 0 and BX = 0 (by postulate 2) then
AX=BX
=
0=0 <---this is true, obviously
QED.


Now find the holes in my proof.

EDIT:extra stuff added.

#195208 87 2006-06-27T10:49:37Z iangb
I'll try and finsh this off.

Kirby:

For my example, one-ninth is a decimal place with an infinite number of ones after it.

You have one-ninth, or 0.1 (repeating)
Double it to 2/9, and every repeating 1 is doubled to 2
Triple it up, and every 1 is tripled to 3. Which makes sense - three ninths = one third = 0.3 (recurring)

Multiply it by nine, and the same principle applies. Every 1 from the 0.1(recurring) is multiplied by 9, to give 0.9(recurring)

As you well know, one ninth multiplied by nine is equal to one. Therefore 0.9(recurring) is equal to one.

(In other words, ^read what bigblargh just wrote^)

Sketch: In chemistry something with a pH or 6.9 would be acidic, but something with a pH of 6.9 (recurring) is neutral (and would be read on the pH meter as a perfect 7).

Wedgie:Infinity is wierder than you think it is.

#9963 1 2006-07-09T21:48:35Z iangb
1.2 version released - see further down the page, here

1.3 released - look here. Have an invert/'shrink' function.

It's been a while since I've programmed anything... so here's something new.

Map Maker 1.1

This program 'grows' a map, based on tile positioning. You can either grow a pre-made tileset, or seed one randomly.

The controls should be obvious - click 'grow (one step)' to advance one step, or click 'grow to finish' to advance as far as possible. To grow a premade tileset, paste map data into the text box and click 'load' before growing. To seed a new map, click the 'seed' button. 'Undo' resets the text one grow back (either one step or to completion).

When clicking 'grow to finish' - be patient, as this may take a good few seconds, depending on your CPU speed. Having N not running/in Boss mode speeds up the process drastically.

The maps made vary in quality, but all make sense and sometimes are rather good indeed. Use, Enjoy, and tell me what you think.

Coming in 1.2 (if I get good feedback/can be bothered):
Level preview box
Expanded tileset area (currently a single-tile border of the map is ignored)
Further suggestions welcome
Straight/curved tiles options (pseudo-worked-around, To Be Improved)
Trackback abilities - hopefully to go back to multiple stages

EDIT:Have a screenshot of an example tileset just made.
EDIT2: More things added to my 'to-do' list for 1.2.

..wow. That took me less time than I thought. Hot on the heels of the first release, comes

Map Maker 1.2
New features:
'Style' option - change tiles in any existing/generated tileset to straight/curved(concave/convex or a mix of the two)/mixed (both straight and curved)

Preview window - See the tileset grow as you click

Advanced trackback option - unlimited (well, up to 1000000) undos/redos. Like the same function in Word, this overwrites itself if you undo then grow. You could probably break this if you tried hard enough, but normal use shouldn't cause a problem, and any problem is solved with a quick quit/restart

I've also removed the 'grow to finish' button, as it takes less time and is easer to control to simply keep clicking until there is no change in the tileset. Loading also now happens automatically.

Comments/Bug reports/Update suggestions are very welcome.

Quote: Guest, 2006-07-23T15:46:03Z
If the earth moves away from the sun a little bit, it will come back
Nuh-uh. Gravity gets weaker as you move further away from the massive object, so if the earth were to move further away from the sun then it would spiral away from it. Similarly if the earth were to move closer to the sun then the earth would eventually go into the sun.

Circular motion and gravity is a real pain.

OK... here's why it actually won't work. Every action has an equal and opposite reaction, yes? So when millions of people jump upwards, the earth will move downwards a little bit, so that momentum is conserved. Then after the high point of the collective jump, not only will the people fall down but the planet will fall back up a tiny amount - the same amount that it moved down by when the people were rising. Then the people meet the earth and all momentum is cancelled out and we are back where we started. No change.

The way that fake highscores are going to be caught is a 'demo verifyer' - a bot that checks highscores by running the map/demo data and comparing the actual final time for the demo with the 'official' time that the demo claims. If it's false, then the highscore is automatically deleted.

The only thing that isn't caught by that is genuine demos that have been made by cheating - fbf or similar. And there ain't a lot that can be done about that, short of encrypting demos as they are made or similar.

#215078 4 2006-08-13T14:58:07Z iangb
Hrmph....

The search for unification is a major one. Simplified, the main difference between general relativity and quantum mechanics is that according to relativity, spacetime is smooth - be it flat or curved. However quantum mechanics describes spacetime on a tiny scale as a 'quantum froth' - totally unpredictable. Normally this doesnt matter because on the tiny scale quantum can apply and on every other scale relativity can apply, but for specific cases such as black holes - massive objects operating on tiny scales - there is a problem.

String theory essentially solves this problem by describing fundamental particles not as infinitely small point-particles, but as loops of energy with a finite width. Because that width is greater than the scale on which the 'quantum froth' operates, it can be ignored completely as it is too small to ever affect matter - by defenition, nothing can ever be smaller than a string-particle.

#230862 246 2006-09-19T22:26:54Z iangb
Two Three parts to my answer. Why I'm agnostic, why I'm atheist, and a middle bit, which is either (most likely) ignorable or the most important part.

Why I'm agnostic:
It's... tricky. You can disprove Christianity based on logic and flaws in the bible - ultimately by applying logic to the bible. But if God exists, and is truly omnipotent, then He trancendes logic, so any logical argument falls foul. Similarly any flaws in the bible are laid aside as 'metaphor', or 'translation problems', or any other features of mankind's inherant corruption. And pretty much everything else falls under the domain of ineffability - just because it doesn't make sense to me doesn't mean that it isn't true.
In short, it's easy to disprove God if you assume first that He doesn't exist. If you assume He does exist, then all of the logic you can come up with is inapplicable.

The middle bit:
It is becoming increasingly hard to define a 'true' christian. There is fundamentalism, which, IMO, is blatantly absurd and, as you say, incredibly harmfull to humanity (allthough, even then, I could be wrong). There are more moderate Christians, those who blindly follow their faith and those like Maximo and to a certain extent Obby (allthough I think that he thinks he knows more than he does), who have looked into their faith and are satisfied with it. Then there are those who beleive in Christ and God, but have distanced themselves from organised religion. Of those three the choice is difficult.
Fundamentalism is, from my current viewpoint, insane (see here for a nice example). But if God does exist and the bible is 100% true, due to unknown God-powers, then it is the only correct path. The moderate path is equally valid if it is correct, and is far less harmfull than fundamentalism. The non-organised-religion path is free from human corruption, but many church-goers would argue that it does not count as true Christianity.
Opinion-wise, I'd say that the more liberal the religion, the better (so non-organised is my favourite). This has nothing to do with proof (to me, all paths are unprovable and undisprovable), but it does aid in choice.

Why I'm atheist:
So, God is unprovable, and un-dis-provable. All that is left is the choice. And I, personally, see no need for God. I see not God, but a God of the Gaps, which humanity has used to explain away all that is currently not understood. And as I want to discover more about the universe, I do not want to be able to just fall back and say "oh, God did it". That's the easy way out. I feel I can live my life well, following my own moral code, without a metaphorical Father allways keeping His eye on me to make sure I obey, or forcing me through pointless ritual.
Oh, and Pascals wager (the only pro-God argument) does not apply because there are many different mutually exclusive religions. They can't all be true.
My main beef (-sic-, heh) with christianity is that it seperates action from faith. To go to heaven, Jesus proclaims, all you have to do is beleive in Christ. Allthough this implies you have to act in a good way, it never states this, nor does it tell you what a 'good' way is - thanks to our good friend the Old Testament and its outdatedness and openness to misinterpretation. I'm never sure I want to be part of a faith where all that matters is your beleifs, not your deeds.

Oh, and on the topic of meeting people for the first time...
This is a (lengthy) quote from a book called Icewind Dale, by R.A. Salvatore. It is suitably geeky/D&D-ish book, and the names won't mean anything to those who don't know the backstory, but the message behind the names and the swords/sorcery is one that I think I now live my life by. If you have the time, read it. It is surely worth it.
Quote
The world is full of ruffians. The world is full of people of good character. Both of these statements are true, I believe, because within most of the people I have known lies the beginning points of both seemingly disparate paths.

Some people are too timid to ever be ruffians, of course, and others too kindhearted, and similarly, some folk are too hard-tempered to ever let their good qualities show. But the emotional make-up of most people lies somewhere in the middle, a shade of gray that can be easily darkened or lightened by simple interaction. Race can certainly alter the shade how well I have seen that since my road led me to the surface! An elf might noticeably flinch at the approach of a dwarf, while a dwarf might do likewise, or even spit upon the ground, if the situation is reversed.

Those initial impressions are sometimes difficult to overcome, and sometimes become lasting, but beyond race and appearance and other things that we cannot control, I have learned that there are definite decisions that I can make concerning which reaction I will edge someone else toward.

The key to it all, I believe, is respect.

When I was in Luskan with Wulfgar, we crossed through a tavern full of ruffians, men who used their fists and weapons on an almost daily basis. Yet, another friend of mine, Captain Deudermont of the Sea Sprite, often frequent such taverns, and rarely, very rarely, ever gets into so much as a verbal argument. Why is this? Why would a man such as Deudermont, obviously (as is shown by his dress and manner) a man of some wealth, and a man of respectable society, as well, not find himself immersed in brawls as regularly as others? He often goes in alone, and stands quietly at the bar, but though he hardly says a word, he surely stands out among the more common patrons.

Is it fears that holds the ruffians from the man? Are they afraid that if they tangle with Deudermont, they will find retribution at the hands of his crew? Or has Deudermont simply brought with him such a reputation for ferocity as to scare off any potential challengers?

Neither, I say. Certainly the captain of the Sea Sprite must be a fine warrior, but that is no deterrent to the thugs of the taverns; indeed, the greatest fighting reputation only invites challenges among those folk. And though Deudermonts crew is formidable, by all accounts, more powerful and connected men that he have been found dead in the gutters of Luskan.

No, what keeps Captain Deudermont safe is his ability to show respect for anyone he mets. He is a man of charm, who holds well his personal pride. He grants respect at the outset of a meeting and continues that respect until the person forfeits it. This is very different that the way most people view the world. Most people insist that respect has to be earned, and with many, I have come to observe, earning it is no easy task! Many, and I include Bruenor and Wulfgar in this group, demand that anyone desiring their friendship first earn their respect, and I can understand their point of view, and once believed that I held one similar.

On my journey to the south on the Sea Sprite, Captain Deudermont taught me better, made me realize, without ever uttering a word on the subject, that demanding of another that he earns your respect is, in of itself, an act of arrogance, a way of self elevation, implying by its very nature that your respect is worth earning.

Deudermont takes the opposite approach, one of acceptance and one lacking initial judgment. This may seem a subtle alternative but it most certainly is not. Would that the man be anointed a king, I say, for he has learned the secret of peace. When Captain Deuermont, dressed in his finery, enters a tavern of common peasant thugs, most within the place, and society at large, would view him as a superior. And yet, in his interactions with these people, there is no air of superiority about the man at all. In his eyes and in his heart, he is among peers, among other intelligent creatures whose paths have led them to a different and not better or worse place than his own. And went Deudermont grants respect to men who would think nothing of cutting his heart out, he disarms them, he takes away whatever reason they might have found to fight with him.

There is much more to it than that, Captain Deudermont is able to do this because he can honestly attempt to see the world thought the eyes of another. He is a man of empathy, a man who revels in the differences of people rather than fearing those differences.

How rich is his life! How full of wonder and how wide of experience!

Captain Deudermont taught these things to me, by example. Respect is one of the most basic need of reasoning creatures, particularly among men. An insult is just that because it is an assault upon respect, upon esteem, and upon that most dangerous of qualities: pride.

So when I meet people now, they do not have to earn my respect. I grant it, willingly and happily, expecting that in doing so I will come to learn that even more about this beautiful world around me, that my experiences will widen.

Certainly some people will see this as a weakness or cowardice, will misconstrue my intentions as sublimation, rather than acceptance of equal worth. But it is not fear that guides my actions I have seen far too much of battle to fear it any longer it is hope.

The hope that I will find another Bruenor, or another Catti-brie, for I have come to know that I can never have too many friends.

So I offer you respect, and it will take much for you to lose it. But if you do, if you choose to see it as weakness and seize upon your perceived advantage, well

Perhaps Ill then lt you talk with Guenhwyvar
