#238804 39 2006-10-09T18:16:22Z iangb
Quote
Schrdinger's cat
In the world of quantum mechanics, the laws of physics that are familiar from the everyday world no longer work. Instead, events are governed by probabilities. A radioactive atom, for example, might decay, emitting an electron, or it might not. It is possible to set up an experiment in such a way that there is a precise fifty-fifty chance that one of the atoms in a lump of radioactive material will decay in a certain time and that a detector will register the decay if it does happen. Schrdinger, as upset as Einstein about the implications of quantum theory, tried to show the absurdity of these implications by imagining such an experiment set up in a closed room, or box, which also contains a live cat and a phial of poison, so arranged that if the radioactive decay does occur then the poison container is broken and the cat dies. In the everyday world, there is a fifty-fifty chance that the cat will be killed, and without looking inside the box we can say, quite happily, that the cat inside is either dead or alive. But now we encounter the strangeness of the quantum world. According to the theory, neither of the two possibilities open to the radioactive material, and therefore to the cat, has any reality unless it is observed. The atomic decay has neither happened nor not happened, the cat has neither been killed nor not killed, until we look inside the box. Theorists who accept the pure version of quantum mechanics say that the cat exists in some indeterminate state, neither dead nor alive, until an observer looks into the box to see how things are getting on. Nothing is real unless it is observed.
The ironical thing is that Schrodinger made up that idea to disprove the idea that "nothing is real until it is observed". People just took it the wrong way.

Anyway... on-topic. I don't think that making an initial assumption based on past experience is an act of faith.
For example, I assume that Dave's fridge contains food. What faith is used then other than that my past experiences with fridges are an accurate guide to my future experiences with fridges? I could be wrong in my assumption - it is impossible to tell the contents of Dave's fridge. But my assumption is not based on faith.

Quote: stepself, 2006-10-23T01:38:26Z
Planck time isn't a product of string theory, it's a necessary consequence of the uncertainty principle and quantum mechanics.
That's not right... is it? Quantum mechanics is flawed (well, it doesn't fit with Relativity) because it has no minimum length scale, and on reeeally tiny lengths spacetime gets a bit... frothy. ST solves that by introducing strings as the minimum length, and from that comes the concept of planck time.
The uncertainty principle just says that knowledge of momentum and position are mutually exclusive, so as you know more about one thing you know less about the other. That makes energy levels quantised, but I didn't think it applied to time.
Feel free to correct me.
#245023 19 2006-10-23T19:06:00Z iangb

So before string theory planck time still existed, but it wasn't the minimum time quanta because particles were treated as points rather than strings, so there was no length quanta. Before string theory, space had to be treaded as the quantum froth, but now the length quanta is greater than the scale on which that froth exists, so it can be ignored, and spacetime becomes smooth and quantised.

Because we make a 'ph' sound in 'phooey', not a 'f' sound. They really are different, but we can't differentiate between them easilly, in the same way that 'r' and 'l' hard to distinguish for someone of asian upbringing.

Try saying 'fish'. Note at the start of the word your front upper teeth are over your lower lip.
Now say 'phooey'. Either your teeth will be behind your lower lip, or you won't be using your teeth at all - you'll be using your upper and lower lips alone to make the sound. We don't easilly notice the difference, but it's there.

#12415 1 2006-11-22T23:22:43Z iangb
Kablizzy mentioned something about this, and as I've been donating a few of my weekends to charity recently I thought I'd share, and maybe encourage others (who can) to do the same.

At my university (and at many UK universities, I don't know about the US), there is an organisation/society called RAG. Officially it stands for Raising And Giving, but that's such a cheesy (and partly misleading) name I don't think it has ever been called that by anyone, ever.

RAG has two aims in life - charity and having fun. This week at uni is RAG week, which means we've been running about all week dressed as giant animals delivering pints, pizzas, roses, porn mags or whatever was requested to lectures, serenading random people and doing sponsered outdoor sleepovers (last night - and if was freezing. I should have stolen a second sleeping bag to go outside the first one). Also throughout the term we run Rag cloakroom at the Students Union, but that's a more minor thing, allthough it makes steady money. For all of these, all proceeds go to charity

The other main event RAG does os a RAG Raid - which take place about every other weekend. We go to a city on Friday, go out Friday night, sleep on a floor somewhere (normally a church floor, allthough last time we blagged a common room which was heated... lovely), collect money all day Saturday, go out again in the evening, then head home on the Sunday to collapse and sleep. It's awesome. So far this term I've been to Manchester and Liverpool, but there have been raids I haven't been able to go to. In the last 8 weeks we've collected over 10,000 for various charitys from raids alone, and had excellent fun while doing it (180 of which has been from me, but I'm not great at collecting - yet). In just under a fortnight we're doing a sponsered hitchike to Dublin for the weekend, which should be excellent - no collecting, but hitching instead, and the same fun nights out.

Other events later in the year include the Big Easy - a giant school fete, and the Rag Blag - start with a small item like a pencil and see if you can swop it for something better (which we then auction off). Last year someone got to a TV in about 10 swops.

My point? Charity is not only a good cause, but it can be fun. If your local school/college/university has a RAG equivalent, join it. If it doesn't, which is very likely for schools, get involved in whatever events you can, and if on the street you see a guy dressed as a giant kangaroo waving a bucket at you in a hopefull manner, give what you can - it might just be me.

Warwick Rag homepage

Any other RAG-ers out there? Is there a US equivlent?

#261196 39 2006-11-28T22:24:48Z iangb
I read the whole of that 'proof', and... it's rubbish. Specifically:

2a - the universe could have undergone infinite acceleration. There is no proof that the speed of light has allways been the top speed of the universe.

3 - not valid because the proof then goes on to say that there exists an 'uncaused cause' (4)
3 a ii - see 2a

4 - (3) says that nothing is uncaused
4 a i - read up on 'chaos theory'. Tiny events can have massive consequences

Everything after that point is based on 3, 4 and 4 a i. 3 and 4 are mutually exclusive and 4ai is incorrect. Oh, and there's the leap in logic that assumes that God is the supernatural bit.

Another general flaw in this is that it treats 'before' the universe exists as a place with dimensions, including time. But 'before' the Big Bang was timeless, spaceless.

Quote: macaddict_17, 2006-11-29T02:36:02Z
Those of us who believe the Universe exists can realize that the universe either had a beginning or it did not. If it didn't have a beginning, the universe must have existed for an infinite amount of time. There are two problems with this: The universe would have reached a state in which all usable energy is gone, and that 'the present' would not be happening, because it takes an infinite amount of time to get to any point on an infinite timeline, and you cannot cross an infinity. Therefore we know that the universe had a beginning.
The current universe had a start, yes. Before that... we don't know. There could be the 'big crunch' scenario, or ther could simply be void - no space or time.

Quote: macaddict_17, 2006-11-29T02:36:02Z
The principle of causualty states that everything that had a beginning had a cause. This is a provable law of logic, not something you can just 'fluke' your way out of. The only way to deny the principle is to deny the existence of logic itself.
Quantum physics doesn't agree with you. According to quantum physics, matter or energy can breifly appear in very tiny quantities, without cause or predictability.
And to define the universe as having a 'beginning' is also fallacious, to a certain extent. If, 'before' the universe existed, there was no time, then the universe did not 'begin'. As soon as Time existed, the universe was there. And to speak about the start of time is illogical - for something to have a start it must have a before and an after, and Time has no 'before'.

Quote: macaddict_17, 2006-11-29T02:36:02Z
Therefore, the universe had a cause. But what about the existence of this cause? Lets call it Cause A. If Cause A had a cause, Cause B, then what caused Cause B? Etc. This is called an infinite regression of causes, an impossibility. Eventually you have to go back to something that had no cause. This something would have therefore had no beginning and existed for an infinite amount of time.
As mentioned before, time 'started' (note the 'quotes') when the universe 'began', so nothing can have existed for an infinite amount of time. And it is possible that the universe has no 'beginning' either - see the big bang/big crunch theory.

Quote: macaddict_17, 2006-11-29T02:36:02Z
But wait: wouldn't this thing have to be outside of space? (not interstellular space, but space as in "matter takes up space".) If it is inside space, it is part of the universe, and cannot have caused the universe. That would be like going back in time and fathering yourself: Its not possible. It is therefore outside space, and outside of time, because time and space are a continuum. (spelling?)
Unless time is a loop (a offset of the big bang/big crunch idea), then yes, your cause must exist 'outside' spacetime, because 'before' the universe there was neither space nor time. Or at least, it cannot exist in the spacetime dimensions that were created in the Big Bang. A consequence of string theory is that the Bang may have been created by 'branes' - 2-dimensional sheets - colliding in a higher dimension.

Quote: macaddict_17, 2006-11-29T02:36:02Z
So we have a thing that has no beginning, it has just been. We know it is outside of space and time, and that it must be greater than the universe. What could this be but God? What else is there that might have caused the world as we know it?
Assuming you're right about the whole 'uncaused cause', one solution as mentioned would be extradimensional branes colliding. Other than that... *shrug*. The edges of possibilities are there, but we don't have the knowledge.

I think that's added some extra... dimensions (heh) to the arguments allready put forwards.

Quote: Me!
Two Three parts to my answer. Why I'm agnostic, why I'm atheist, and a middle bit, which is either (most likely) ignorable or the most important part.

Why I'm agnostic:
It's... tricky. You can disprove Christianity based on logic and flaws in the bible - ultimately by applying logic to the bible. But if God exists, and is truly omnipotent, then He trancendes logic, so any logical argument falls foul. Similarly any flaws in the bible are laid aside as 'metaphor', or 'translation problems', or any other features of mankind's inherant corruption. And pretty much everything else falls under the domain of ineffability - just because it doesn't make sense to me doesn't mean that it isn't true.
In short, it's easy to disprove God if you assume first that He doesn't exist. If you assume He does exist, then all of the logic you can come up with is inapplicable.

The middle bit:
It is becoming increasingly hard to define a 'true' christian. There is fundamentalism, which, IMO, is blatantly absurd and, as you say, incredibly harmfull to humanity (allthough, even then, I could be wrong). There are more moderate Christians, those who blindly follow their faith and those like Maximo and to a certain extent Obby (allthough I think that he thinks he knows more than he does), who have looked into their faith and are satisfied with it. Then there are those who beleive in Christ and God, but have distanced themselves from organised religion. Of those three the choice is difficult.
Fundamentalism is, from my current viewpoint, insane (see here for a nice example). But if God does exist and the bible is 100% true, due to unknown God-powers, then it is the only correct path. The moderate path is equally valid if it is correct, and is far less harmfull than fundamentalism. The non-organised-religion path is free from human corruption, but many church-goers would argue that it does not count as true Christianity.
Opinion-wise, I'd say that the more liberal the religion, the better (so non-organised is my favourite). This has nothing to do with proof (to me, all paths are unprovable and undisprovable), but it does aid in choice.

Why I'm atheist:
So, God is unprovable, and un-dis-provable. All that is left is the choice. And I, personally, see no need for God. I see not God, but a God of the Gaps, which humanity has used to explain away all that is currently not understood. And as I want to discover more about the universe, I do not want to be able to just fall back and say "oh, God did it". That's the easy way out. I feel I can live my life well, following my own moral code, without a metaphorical Father allways keeping His eye on me to make sure I obey, or forcing me through pointless ritual.
Oh, and Pascals wager (the only pro-God argument) does not apply because there are many different mutually exclusive religions. They can't all be true.
My main beef (-sic-, heh) with christianity is that it seperates action from faith. To go to heaven, Jesus proclaims, all you have to do is beleive in Christ. Allthough this implies you have to act in a good way, it never states this, nor does it tell you what a 'good' way is - thanks to our good friend the Old Testament and its outdatedness and openness to misinterpretation. I'm never sure I want to be part of a faith where all that matters is your beleifs, not your deeds.

Quote: Tsukatu, 2006-12-05T20:01:37Z
But... don't you want to believe what's true?
See, that's the thing. Define 'true'. It's the kind of thinking I like.

Love is real, it true, but it doesn't physically exist. The same goes for 'boredom', 'hope', 'enjoyment', 'justice' and 'free will' (maybe). All are man-made constructs, and only make sense from a human point of view. But you have to beleive in them. And all religions are true, for a given value of 'true'.

Alternately, science and the physical world doesn't know, doesn't mind, doesn't care if you believe in it or not. And it will far outlast any religion. And science never claims to be 'true'. ID supporters like to bring up that evolution, unlike something like gravity, is just a theory. But apart from the obvious reply (evolution is the theory that fits the observable evidence the best), there is also the fact that gravity is equally only a theory. In reality, Newtons laws of gravity (which are the ones used pretty much everywhere) aren't quite correct - the orbit of Mercury doesn't follow a Newtonian orbit. Instead we had to come up with a new, more complicated way of describing how gravity works - in this case using Einstein's General Relativity. And even that is probably not 100% correct - see problems involving GR and quantum mechanics.

So... the only things that are real - science and the natural physical observable universe - are not allways 'true'. And the only things that are 'true' - human-created concepts such as beauty and tiredness - are not real. Where does that leave faith?

Like you, I don't know the answer. I just see the universe and try to understand it as best I can. It could be, as you said, that we were created by a now-apathetic deity. It could be we are all an experiment being carried out by a hyper-intelligent shade of the colour blue, or the we are all in a computer-generated world created by slightly incompetent robots. Unless that has an effect on my life, I'm not too worried. The only thing I can be sure of is: here and now, we are alive. Best to make the most of it, then.

#267538 5 2006-12-10T12:31:35Z iangb
This seems to be my standard answer to most things, but Free will... may or may not exist, and it is impossible to say. At the moment, thanks to quantum mechanics, there is a level of uncertanty in the universe - put a particle in a box and you have no idea at any one time where the particle is in that box, or even if it has stayed there. It could be that at a quantum level the human Mind (where there is a capital M it's a M for Metaphysics) can influence the universe to manifest free will.
At the moment, there is no physical explanation for the workings of the human Mind (as an aside, never ever watch What the Bleep do we know? - a film attempting to 'prove' links between quantum and 'mind powers' - unless you watch it remembering all the way through that it is pretty much 100% fictional and equally bogus)

The alternative is that of a deterministic clockwork universe. Everything that makes up the universe follows the rules, so if you somehow knew the exact position, identity and velocity of each particle in the universe then you could work out all future states of said universe - including the workings of the brain. This alternative may well be the case.
Take an example, on the macroscopic scale - I wake up in the morning, and decide to have corn flakes for breakfast instead of toast. A bunch of factors go into me making my decision - that I've had toast for the last few days, that there was an advert for corn flakes on the radio just as I was waking up, that the box was closest to me when I walked into the kitchen. If the universe was replayed exaclty, from the time of my waking up, all those factors would still appy, and I would still choose to eat corn flakes.
If I had to pick a random number... any psychologist/amatuer magician (go Derren Brown!) will tell you that there is no such thing as random, when it comes to the human mind's ability to choose things. I instinctively allways choose "7" as a number (because of a book I once read) before remembering clearly that it isn't a 'random' number and chosing something alse - but my new choice has, no doubt, been affected in some way by previous events. That's how Derren (if you haven't heard of him, you should) does a lot of his 'psychic' tricks - by subliminally suggesting an outcome befor the person even has a chance to pick the 'two of clubs'.

EDIT: This lack of free will is by no means a bad thing. In a very real way, you are in control of yuor own destiny - if you lost the match it was because you felt lazy and thought you coud use determinism as an excuse to get out of it, or because the other team was better than you (think about it - if, for example, a bunch of pre-teens were to have a match against the UK football squad then, in an equally real sense, the outcome of the match would be predetermined - the preteens are never going to win apart from in very bad kids movies). Just because what you chose to do is pre-determined doesn't mean that you aren't making a choice.
And just because your future is predetermined, doesn't mean that it is predictable. The only way to predict the future outcome of a system with 100% accuracy is... well at the moment it is impossibe due to Heisneburg's Uncertanty Principle, but if you could somehow get around that then you could only predict the future of a system if you were completely removed from the system - otherwise you would have to read a prediction involving yourself, which is impossible (once you know your own future, you can chose to change it). As everything in the universe affects (on at least a minute scale) everything else, to predict the future you would need to predict the futture state of the entire universe, which means that you would need to be outside the universe.
Equally if you were to go back in time repeatedly to see if I would allways chose corn flakes, then that would break the system - it only applies if the universe is replayed exactly. Your presence could mess up my decision, even if I don't see you - for example you open a door to get into my house, meaning that it's a bit colder so I want some nice warm toast.

#269968 12 2006-12-14T11:02:56Z iangb
I know the idea - 'tis a flawed paradox. Highlight my post for the flaw, if you don't want to try working it out on your own.

Imagine the path of the fly, in terms of it's speed relative to the ground.

It starts off flying to the left, then splats onto the train and starts moving to the right. Obviously it doesn't start to slow down until it is in contact with the train. So (goes the argument), at some point, the fly that is touching the train is (for an instantanious length of time) stationary relative to the ground. But since it is touching the train at that time this must mean that the train is stationary relative to the fly, and therefore also stationary relative to the ground. For that instant then, the train is stationary.

Answer:
It only works because it treats a fly as an incompressable object.
If, however, you treat the fly as a compressable object which is compressing (read: splatting) all the while that it is de/reaccelerating to the speed of the train, then there isn't a problem. The train isn't stationary relative to the fly until the fly has stopped it's rapid change in velocity, at which point it is going at the speed of the train anyway.

Quote: macaddict_17, 2006-12-20T20:11:14Z
Then how come nobody can come up with any evidence to that one guy's questions?
I did, but you said it doesn't count. I'll give you another... one that nicely deals with 'irriducable complexity'.

A while ago (~1993), an engineer called Adrian Thompson decided to breed circuits. Computer science sometimes uses a 'genetic algorithm' to breed computer programs - this works by combining different algorithms (synonymous with DNA) in multiple ways and taking the best, then recombining. Thompson wanted to try this system with electronics.
Rather than modelling the whole thing on a computer, he used 'logic cells' - essentially chips containing many many logic gates. He decided on a task - to create a circuit that could distinguish between input frequencies of 10kHz and 100kHz, and give a relevant output. He started with 100 logic cells, and used a computer to randomly create 50 'instruction codes' for the cells. He then 'bred' the instructions, and killed off all but the 50 most succesfull results, and recombined them.
After 4100 such breedings, a solution was arrived at which gave no output for an input of 10kHz, and a 5V output when 100kHz was fed in. And the arrangement of logic cells was one which no human engineer could have come up with - of the 100 logic cells only 32 were used, and 5 of those were necessary but were not connected electronically to the rest of the circuit - presumably they created magnetic fields by which the circuit worked, or something. Thompson (the creator) described it as 'Really, I don't have the faintest idea how it works'.

So irriducable complexity can be physically acheived through the process of evolution - mutations and selection. That proof enough for you?

On transitionary fossils - this is minor, but have a quote
Quote: Catherine Howard
"There are many excellent transitionary fossils," I said. "But the creationists will never accept that, because they have decided, a priori, that there is no such thing. It works like this: whenever we show them a transitionary fossil, B, between two other fossils, A and C, the creationists simply say that B is close enough to A to be the same 'kind,' or far enough away to be a different kind. Either that, or they say that there are now two gaps that must be filled, between A and B, and between B and C.
Every fossil is a transitionary fossil - on the most basic scale between that fossils' parents and it's immediate offspring. Today's animals are not the 'final' product of evolution - in a few millenia todays animals will be transitionary before the animals we will have then.

On observational/Historical science - We can observe (micro)evolution in action today. For example - virii mutating (and bacterium too - just in case you thought I'd forgotten about them).
My point was this: evolution explains the observable facts in the best scientific manner we have yet to come up with. Even though it is 'just a theory', even if it fails to explain every single thing in nature, it is perfectly acceptable - just as Newton's Gravity is acceptable.
Oh, and I liked the Santa analogy. It reminded me of mankinds search for God in 'the heavens' above us (cf the Tower of Babel story).

On irriducable complexity - Firstly, you've said that you can't define 'complexity'. Secondly, I've shown you that irriducable complexity can occur - both in bacteria flagellum (that evil-looking document I linked to) and in the case of the microchips (which Atilla re-explained nicely).

On the microchips/'Computer modeling - in each stage of the process, the circuit was better or equal at completing the task set than it's predecessor. The only reason 'human intelligence' is used is because, as I said, in a lab there is no natural external pressure on the organism/circuit to survive/compete. The only way to replicate such a pressure is to use human, or programed, intelligence. Again, in the model of the eye, each stage was better at light-sensing than previously - the model wasn't trying to become like the eye, it was trying to become better at seeing - and the eye was a natural result of that.

On information/mutation - incidentally, the bits in the frogs DNA are relevant. They are because, unlike most conditions that mammals survive in, a frog's conditions can change wildly. So while a mammals DNA says 'always make enzyme A', a frog's has to say 'if temperature = 10-20 degrees, make Enzyme A. If temperature = 20-30 degrees, make Enzyme B. If temp... etc.'
You are confusing 'information' with 'meaning'. Here's why (paraphrased from science of discworld 2):
There are two ways of measuring information contained in a signal - Shannon and Chaitin. Shannon's (the easy one) information measure "puts a number to the extent to which our uncertanty about the bits that make up the signal is reduced by what we receive". So if the signal is in the form of a binary code, the signal 100101 contains 6 bits of information, as does the signal 010101 and 111111. Chaitans information measure is, basically, about how compressable the message is - so 111111 has less Chaitan information than 010101, which has less information than 100101. "It is curious that 'To be or not to be' contains the same Shannon information, and less Chaitan information than 'xyQGRlfryu&d%sk0wc'. The reason for this is that information is not the same as meaning.
...
So far, no-one has been able to come up with an algorithm for the meaning content of a signal
When a gene mutates, the information increaces (or stays the same). The meaning, however, changes - sometimes for better, sometimes for worse. Then natural selection kicks in and all you have left is beneficial mutations.

1: A quote. [these bits added by me]

The ID movement has opened my eyes. I realise that allthough I beleive evolution explains why the living world is the way it is, I can't actually prove it. 2: Of this explanation of evolution, which bit do you disagree with? (quoted from science of discworld 3, which i got for Christmas and haven't quite finished reading yet)
Quote
Breifly, Darwin's theory goes like this.
1. Organisms, even those in the same species, are variable. Some are bigger than others, or bolder than others, or prettier than others.
2. This variability is to some extent hereditary, passed on to offspring.
3. Unchecked population growth would quickly exhaust the capacity of the planet, so something checks it - competition for limited rescources.
4. Therefore as time passes, the organisms that do survive long enough to breed will be modified in ways that improve their chance of surviving to breed - a process called natural selection.
5. Ongoing small changes can lead, in the long run, to big differences
6. The long run has been very long indeed - hundreds of millions of years, maybe more. So by now those differences can have become huge.

On the subject of evolving irriducible complexity, I'm going to paraphrase Science of Discworld 3 again.
Quote
"The deduction that an irreducably compex system cannot evolve is valid only if evolution only consists of adding new parts. If this was the case, it would be obviously true: look at a complex system as the final 'step', remove a component and get a failed organism. However, evolution need not merely add on identifiable components like a factory-worker assembling a machine. It can also remove them, or the entire structure can evolve in parallel. Also, 'fail' is a slippery concept. A watch without hands is useless for telling the time, but it can still be used to set of a bomb, or used on the end of a plumb-line. Organs and biochemical systems often change their functions over time, as we've just seen in the case of the eye [I'm not typing that bit out, instead I recommend you buy/read the book]. For example, removing parts from the bacteria flagellum does not cause it to 'fail'. A previous 'step' in the evolution of the flagellum was a 'type III secretory system' - part of the mechanism by which one bacteria attacks another. A perfecly valid molecule, but nothing to do with propulsion - until the final protein was added, and bacteria made use of it's old attack mechanism to move about.

So... if you want an animal that is half-bird, half dinosaur - I give you Archaeopteryx. Or one of the other toothed/feathered denizens of that era. Or Lucy, who (even if she was found a bit 'scattered'), still had to have existed. Even if archaeologists have been piecing random bones together, an animal must have existed at some time with a skull like that.

If you want an organ that is 'transitional', don't expect to see a half-bellows lung any time soon. We can, however, show you other 'transitional' organs.

Quote
Natural selection removes information
No. Well, sometimes it does, but only when the mutation that caused a defeceit in information was a beneficial one.
Just to clarify, there are two different processes going on here - mutation/breeding and selection. Mutation/breeding can either increase, decreace or unaffect the amount of information contained in DNA. It also changes (or not) the meaning of that information in the DNA - as badly analogied in 'spelling' by you and me and PBS (as an aside, I love the way in your post above that you bought up PBS to support your 'spelling' analogy and then tried to ridicule me for bringing up the vast majority of the scientific community to support evolution). But 'spelling' is a really bad analogy, because molecules are just... different. Consider... well, a relatively simple organic molecule like hexane. It has 6 carbon atoms and 14 hydrogen atoms. If you insist that all the atoms are used, and that they only form a single molecule, there are 6 possible molecules I can think of that use all those atoms, in various combinations, with various (different) properties. If you relax the conditions, that number increaces massivly. And if you swop a hydrogen atom for, say, a sodium atom, you get even more possible combination. And most proteins in the body are hundreds of carbon atoms long, with many extra elements 'added in'. The possible viable ways in which possible proteins can be made is huge, and allthough DNA is long enough that some mutations to it will 'break' a protein, some mutations will also be beneficial. I defy you to find me words that have as much malleability as hexane does, which can be put together in many different ways (the only example I can think of is 'evil', which is an anagram of 'live', 'veil' and 'vile'). Of course there are more names than molecules (allthough technically there is an infinite number of both), because chemistry has created a very good nomenclaure, so the various molecules of C6H14 are hexane, 2 methyl pentane, 3 methyl pentane, 2 3 di-methyl butane, 2 2 di-methyl butane and propyl butane (wow, it's been a good few years since I've done organic chemistry, and I still remember. Huzzah). But that doesn't mean that you can relate molecules to words.

Than comes the second part of evolution - selection. Selection, well, it selects the organisms that are the best. It dosen't affect the specific informational content of those individual organisms at all, it only affects the average informational content of a member of a species. If the beneficial mutation is an increace in information, then natural selection will increase the average information in the population by killing off the 'less informed' members. If the mutation is a decreace in information, then the average content also decreaces.
Your dog example, then (allthough it is very slightly wrong - actually evolution causes extra-long-hair alleas tobe selected, should they mutate that way), is spot on. Mankind is breeding dogs that has less information, and microevolution - which in this case takes significantly less time becuse mutation/breeding is more likely to decreace information than to decreace it - provides.
However, microevolution in the case of bacteria mutating to become resistant to vaccines is the opposite - an increase in information as the bacteria becomes more complex. It just take a short length of time because of two reasons - because bacteria breed very fast from generation to generation, and because when vaccines are around evolutionary pressure is very high on bacteria to survive at all.

Quote: R.A Salvatore @ Icewind Dale trilogy
I am dying.

Every day, with every breath I draw, I am closer to the end of my life.  For we are born with a finite number of breaths, and each one I take edges the sunlight that is my life toward the inevitable dusk.

It is a difficult thing to remember, especially while we are in the health and strength of our youth, and yet, I have come to know that it is an important thing to keep in mind--not to complain or to make melancholy, but simply because only with the honest knowledge that one day I will die can I ever truly begin to live.  Certainly I do not dwell on the reality of my own mortality, but I believe that a person cannot help but dwell, at least subconsciously, on that most imposing specter until he has come to understand, to truly understand and appreciate, that he will one day die.  That he will one day be gone from this place, this life, this consciousness and existence, to whatever it is that awaits.  For only when a person completely and honestly accepts the inevitability of death is he free of the fear of it.

So many people, it seems, stick themselves into the same routines, going through each day's rituals with almost religious precision.  They become creatures of simple habit.  Part of that is the comfort afforded by familiarity, but there is another aspect to it, a deep-rooted belief that as long as they keep everything the same, everything will remain the same.  Such rituals are a way to control the world about them, but in truth, they cannot.  For even if they follow the exact routine day after day after day, death will surely find them.

I have seen other people paralyze their entire existence around that greatest of mysteries, shaping their every movement, their every word, in a desperate attempt to find the answers to the unanswerable.  They fool themselves, either through their interpretations of ancient texts or through some obscure sign from a natural event, into believing that they have found the ultimate truth, and thus, if they behave accordingly concerning that truth, they will surely be rewarded in the afterlife.  This must be the greatest manifestation of that fear of death, the errant belief that we can somehow shape and decorate eternity itself, that we can curtain its windows and place its furniture in accordance with our own desperate desires.

I believe them to be wrong, though in truth, I cannot know anything for certain concerning what mystery lies beyond this mortal coil.  And so I, too, am but a creature of faith and hope.

Perhaps the greatest evil I see in this existence is when supposedly holy men prey upon the basic fears of death of the common folk to take from them.  "Give to the church!" they cry.  "Only then will you find salvation!"  Even more subtle are the many religions that do not directly ask for a person's money, but insist that anyone of goodly and godly heart who is destined for their particular description of heaven, would willingly give that money over.

And of course, the world is ripe with "doomsayers," people who claim that the end of the world is at hand, and cry for repentance and for almost slavish dedication.

I can only look at it all and sigh, for as death is the greatest mystery, so it is the most personal of revelations.  We will not know, none of us, until the moment it is upon us, and we cannot truly and in good conscience convince another of our beliefs.

It is a road we travel alone, but a road that I no longer fear, for in accepting the inevitable, I have freed myself from it.  In coming to recognize my mortality, I have found the secret to enjoying those centuries, years, months, days, or even hours, that I have left to draw breath.  This is the existence I can control, and to throw away the precious hours over fear of the inevitable is a foolish thing indeed  And to subconsciously think ourselves immortal, and thus not appreciate those precious few hours that we all have, is equally foolish.

I cannot control the truth of death, whatever my desperation.  I can only make certain that those moments of my life I have remaining are as rich as they can be.

***Marked***

#287102 25 2007-01-18T11:26:51Z iangb
just as a thought... imagine you have an object with positive mass (m1), and an (impossible) object with an equal but negative mass (m2). The force between the two objects would be equal and opposite on each, as usual:
f = g(m1m2)/(r)
if m1 = -m2
f = -g(m1)/(r)

So the force on both m1 and m2 is negative. Now, imagine the effect which that force will have. f=ma so a=f/m, so...

for m1 (+ve mass)
a=f/m1 = -g(m1)/(r)

for m2 (-ve mass, = -m1)
a=f/m2 = -f/m1 = +g(m1)/(r)

So m1 will accelerate away from m2, but m2 will accelerate with equal magnitude towards m1. Wham, perpetual motion, energy from nothing, breaking ALL THE RULES. It makes my head hurt thinking about it.

EDIT: technically that situation isn't rule-breaking (possibly, it's a bit dodgy) because the sum of the system has zero mass, so the system has no centre of mass (or the system's centre of mass is simultaniously every point in the universe), so it isn't really moving, as such.
On the other hand, I'd hate to think about a situation where |m1|>|m2|.

OK... six problems of the fossil record. They were in the whopping 4000-word post of your that, while I didn't TLDR, may not have have been completely taken in. To clarify, they were:
Quote: macaddict_17, 2007-01-05T21:45:28Z
So here is a list with the problems of the fossil record for evolution, alphabetized for your convenience.
1. Abrupt appearance of complex forms
2. Abrupt appearance of all major modern phyla at roughly the same time period (The Cambrian Explosion)
3. Absence of any transitional fossils.
4. Completeness of the fossil record, as far as we can know.
5. Stasis, or unchanging forms, is the rule and not the exception.
6. Unique species with no fossil ancestors.
Most of these reply are going to be similar, so I'll start with a main point. How good do you think the fossil record is? Answer: severely lacking. Before Jurrasic Park gave archaeology glamour, there were precisely 3 fossils of Tyrannosaurus Rex, which had been initially 'laid down' over a seperation time of 5 million years (assuming you don't beleive in a 6000-year old universe, which would make the concept of 5 million years a mite tricky). With that in mind...

1:Abrupt appearence of complex forms.
Not... really. We have all sorts of forms, from the first Ediacarans (possibly 1-1.2 billion years old, no anus or other orifice... essentially big clumps of algae), through to the introduction of triploblasts (animals that had defined organs, about 540-640 million years ago), and so on, and so forth.
Incidentally, it's more the appearance of a complex form. For example, the hand/foot/claw/wing/flipper all share a remarkable similar bone structure.

2. Abrupt appearance of all major modern phyla at roughly the same time period (The Cambrian Explosion)
Easy. Evolution had a new trick, and suddenly it was exploited by everything. From a single source many of the potential mutations stored up for the last few million years - mutations that had no effect until the right conditions were met - suddenly came into effect.
In modern day a (slightly) similar case occured. Reserchers around Chernobyl found five-limbed frogs croaking downwind from the accident site, and claimed to have discovered the effects of radiation mutation. Then they discovered similar mutations upwind from the site, which was free of contamination. The reason was that the blast had killed all of the local predators, so suddenly most of the hundreds of frog eggs were actually surviving, and with no evolutionary pressure the odd mutations weren't being killed off, but instead were living and being discovered.

3: Absence of any transitionary fossils.
We've been over this one. And still not come to any agreement. For transitional fossils in the strictest terms, look for archaeopteryx, the other feather'd beasts from China, the 'human ancestors', the various animals in that 'evolution of the horse' thingy I posted... and every fossil that had ever existed. In fact, Wikipedia to the rescue!
For transitional organ fossils, there are examples of changing teeth, eyes and limbs in various creatures (see the 'horse' article for teeth and limbs). Also, evolution of many 'irreducibly complex' organs have been modelled, to variouslevels of detail (into which I refuse to go).

4. Completeness of the fossil record, as far as we can know.
How does this aid you? The fossil record is far, far, faaaaaaar from complete. All we can know is that the creatures whose fossils we found must have existed, unless God is playing an innfable joke on us (commonly referred to as 'silly buggers')

5. Stasis, or unchanging forms, is the rule and not the exception.
If the exception exists, then that supports evolution. It just means that we have to allow a lot of time for it to have happened in - which, coincidentally, we do have. Please bring on the young earth thingy... especially now I've re-read some of your earlier posts and the site you referenced used the Grand Canyon as evidence.

6. Unique species with no fossil ancestors.
Is this not the same as point #1? Anyway... either reply to it as I did to that point, or reference the huge gaps in the fossil record, the choice is yours...

Done!

so... answers. Really really short version, as I'm still rather ill, I have a maths assignment in tomo... today, and its 2:30AM.
in-post edit: i knew I shouldn't have gone to answer this now... I have a nasty feeling this is going to be longer that I wanted it to be.

Atheism/Antitheism: basically, read Tsukatu's post. I guess, with your semantics, you would indeed call all atheists 'antitheists' and call all agnostic atheists 'atheists'. Unfortunately, that's not what the rest of us refer to them as.
To calrify the clarification: Atheists do not beleive. Antitheists are opposed to beleif.

Sea salt: I really need time, so I'll just do this one in detail. There are several flaws, some bigger than others.

1.) According to your linked article (the later one), the study caps the maximum age of the oceans at 65 million years. It's hardly support for a 6000-year-old earth.

2.) The report states "The known and conjectured processes which deliver and remove dissolved sodium (Na+). to and from the ocean are inventoried." (bold added by me). That critical word: Conjecture(d)
Quote: Conjecture @ dictionary.com
1. the formation or expression of an opinion or theory without sufficient evidence for proof.
2. an opinion or theory so formed or expressed; guess; speculation.
3. Obsolete. the interpretation of signs or omens.
4. to conclude or suppose from grounds or evidence insufficient to ensure reliability.
Of the factors given in the report, whether each is conjecture or not is not stated.

3.)The table of factors references the Cretatious period in it's model. Without an older-than-6000 earth, there is no time for there to have been a cretacious period.

4.)In fact, the report doesn't fit with YEC at all. Look at the graph, found on the bottom of the report.
Note that for the YEC model to be true, the rate of salt accumilation would have to be far, far, far higher (factor of about 1000) than that of today.

5.) The report says that "Nearly one hundred years ago John Joly [2] measured the amount of Na+ dissolved in river water and estimated with extraordinary accuracy... Joly said it would take 80 to 90 million years for the sea to accumulate its present amount of Na+, ".
Comparing 80-90 million years with the reports version of ~65 million years and calling it 'extrodinarilly accurate' seems a bit far-fetched. Nit-picky, but true. I really bring it up because it is designed to encourage the reader to accept the proposed timescale 'because it's amazingly close to the readings from 100 years ago, which were amazingly accurate'.

6.) I can think of at least one unconsidered salt loss factor - total evaporation. Not evaporation as in sea-spray-from-waves, but the kind of evaporation the produces salt mines and the Dead Sea. A fairly significant amount.

So, in short... the report is based on an unknown amount of conjecture, is weasely worded(I may have just made up that term... wow), is at least partly incorrect, and is irrelevant (and even potentially harmfull) to YEC even if it is 100% true.

#303288 6 2007-03-07T19:10:53Z iangb
I think I might know what you mean. Occasionally I feel the same way - that if people aren't with me, then it's because they are purposely avoiding me. I know it's paranoia mixed with ego, and that makes it worse.
The simple answer, I think, is to go out and find the people you like - go to them rather than hoping that they'll come your way. All you need is a couple of awkward moments while you discover about each other, and then you're set up with countless talking points - over shared intrests, things you know they like, events that affect you both, etc...
For me, in a couple of cases I think the problem was I was used to having one or two really close friends at school and not much else. It took me a while to get used to a large social group which might accidentally not include me just because it was too big, so I took each case personally as 'exclusion' and fretted overly about people's opinions of me. Once I realised that I was accepted, and that the same happend from time to time to everyone else, it all became much easier.

Beyond that... you are who you are. If people can't see that, it's their loss, not yours. Smile and nod, and pass on to those who can see that your personality is always your most beautiful feature.

Way back then, there may have been many species. Some died out, the ones that didn't became the horses we know today.

Quote: AiG
Rather, the fossil fragments have been gathered from several continents on the assumption of evolutionary progress, and then used to support the assumption. This is circular reasoning, and does not qualify as objective science.
"Oh, this skeleton looks similar to this one, even though they're from different parts of the world. I wonder if they're from related species?" is equally as valid as "I need something that looks horse-y... that one will do". We don't know which one of those was actually true.

Quote: AiG
The theory of horse evolution has very serious genetic problems to overcome. How do we explain the variations in the numbers of ribs and lumbar vertebrae within the imagined evolutionary progression? For example, the number of ribs in the supposedly 'intermediate' stages of the horse varies from 15 to 19 and then finally settles at 18. The number of lumbar vertebrae also allegedly swings from six to eight and then returns to six again.
This is a problem with AiG assigning evolution with a specific purpose. There is no reason why the path from two distantly related animals - 'distant' being millions of years - should be a smooth one. Evolution did not 'aim' for a specific number of ribs, and then stick with it - rather mutations came and were later replaced.
Plus, changing number of bones is a highly possible mutation - there is a genetic mutation in africa leading to stories of a 'two-toed tribe' -
Quote
Some of the Vadoma have a most unusual deformity of the feet and from this comes the tale of a "two-toed tribe". There is no truth in this as only a few (usually related) individuals suffer from this genetic inheritance, which has deprived them of the middle three toes leaving a foot looking more like that of an ostrich than that of a human. The deformity does not handicap them in any way, and it is said that it assists them in climbing trees.
Just looking at the bolded part, you can see that back in a world full of evolutionary pressure, this advantage could have led to certain members of the tribe survivng, and passing on their mutation, which would spread due to the advantage it gives. Later on, when the trees were more sparse and humanity had returned to plains-dwelling, a different mutation could return some of the toes back to the tribe, which would give them advantagous ballance - and suddenly humanity has gone from 5 toes to 2 and back up to some other number, gaining an advantage every time.

Quote: AiG
Finally, when evolutionists assume that the horse has grown progressively in size over millions of years, what they forget is that modern horses vary enormously in size. The largest horse today is the Clydesdale; the smallest is the Fallabella, which stands at 43 centimetres (17 inches) tall. Both are members of the same species, and neither has evolved from the other.
Just as recently humanity has bred dogs from a single ancestor into a vast multitude of forms, so have we bred horses for different purposes - and this affects the size drastically, just as a chihuahua differs from a great dane. Before human intervention, however, it's likely that horses were much more uniform in size, just as wolves were/are.

It's a case of 'what was there before the universe', keron.

All we know for sure (allthough Macaddict would probably disagree with me on this) is that several billion years ago (give or take a few million), space and time as we currently understand them originated from a singularity (or near-singularity) event, commonly known as the Big Bang. 'Before' that (and now terms like 'before' get a little tricky)... the most popular theory is that there was void, in the truest sense - no space or time - not vacuum, but no actual space for a vaccum to be in, or time in which it can exist. However, another theory is that there was another universe before our current one, which suffered a 'big crunch' (gravity overcomes everything and the universe returns so a singularity state), triggering our own Big bang. That theory means that there need be no 'start' to time - it would just be a repeating loop, with a big bang/crunch starting the whole thing over again. There would be no 'uncaused cause' - the whole thing would just recurr.
It's also possible that each of the previous universes (should they have existed) had different physical constants, meaning that the life-supportingness of our universe does not make it 'special', it just makes it an inevitable consequence of an infintely changing universe.

Obby didn't like this because our current universe appears to be accelerating in it's expansion, and not slowing down. This suggests that either the crunch/bang theory is definitely wrong, or that there is still a lot we don't know about the universe. Personally, I'm going with the second option. I can argue a bunch of reasons with Obby if he wants, but right now I feel like I've typed enough.

#304837 706 2007-03-13T01:33:51Z iangb
On current... there are two types. 'Conventional' current and 'actual' current. 'Actual' current is the flow of electrons, which move from negative to positive, in accordance with electromagnetism. However, 'conventional' current is the opposite - this moves from positive to negative, and is the one which is generally used (for example in a circuit diagram a diode 'points' in the direction of conventional current). The best way to describe conventional current is... well, see below.

Here is a ASCII version of a wire, changing over time. A '-' is an electron, a '_' is plain wire, (no electron), and (-)/(+) are positive/negative terminals.

(-)-----_(+)
(-)----_-(+)
(-)---_--(+)
(-)--_---(+)
(-)-_----(+)
(-)_-----(+)

You can see that as time passes, the electrons are all attracted to - and move towards - the positive terminal. However, the 'gap' (the '_') moves towards the negative terminal. This is the source of (or, if not that, at least a good way of thinking about) 'conventional' current.

If you want an easier way to remember it, just remember that 'conventional' goes in the opposite direction to 'actual'.

No part "evolves for a purpose" - there are just things that change randomly, and then the environment determines if they're usefull or not. You're assigning evolution with 'purpose' again - which is a misunderstanding of what evolution is.
Just so you don't accuse me of question-dodging, I'll answer a correctly-worded version - "can you show me any example of an animal part which has changed it's function as it evolves further?".
The simple answer is yes- there are plenty of examples. For example, part of some virii's DNA includes coding for proteins that prevent the host from recognising the virus as a foreign body, so the host accepts the virus rather than rejecting it. Also, some virii ('symbiotic polydna virii') also function by copying themselves, or bits or themselves, directly into the hosts DNA, and are thus reproduced when that DNA is 'activated' into RNA by the body. The human genome contains a complete copy of just one viral genome - alebeit split up into 3 or 4 seperate section (called 'ERV-3, allthough this is irrelevant). The protein created by part of ERV-3 genome (normally used by the virus to stop the host from rejecting it) is instead used by the human body to stop foetuses in the womb from being recognised as foreign (half of it comes from the father, after all) and rejected by the mother (in addition to other proteins the mother produced pre-virus).

In short, the self-defence mechanism of the virus was implanted in early human DNA by the virus' method of reproduction. Because of evolution (mothers whose bodies were less likely to reject their children obviously had more children) the virus DNA stayed there - with it's function changed to aid in the human reproduction process.

Unfortunately, Mac has done research, but with an agenda in mind, which kinda negates things a little.

On an incidental note, I just though back about what you were saying about ' you can't disprove evolution with an eventual purpose'. And you really can. The main principle of evolution is that when a mutation manifests itself it is tested out in the immediate environment, and if it conveys an advantage then it survives. The immediate environment. Not 'the world as it will be in several thousand years'. Talking about changes with a purpose, then, is not talking about evolution as it is ever defined - instead it is talking about Inteligent design, which is a whole nother kettle of fish.

And speaking of fish, another flaw in YEC for you. If the ocean has become more and more salty, as you claim, the fish in it must have evolved to adapt to the increace in salinity - as putting a freshwater fish in salt water will kill it fairly fast. Even if you discarded that argument and went for a totally unchanging salinity, either all the freshwater fish or all the saltwater fish would have died at the time of the Flood, when for a breif length of time all waters must have had the same salinity.
In short, fish must have evolved since the time of the Flood, should it have existed.

Finally, a quote - partially relevant to 'purpose', partially relevant to the greater discussion in general.

Quote: On the 'watchmaker' analogy @ Darwins Watch
When you see a watch, don not think of hooking up springs and adding cogwheels from some standard box of spare parts. Think instead of a watch whose cogwheels can change shape, grow new teeth, and whose axles and supports evolve along with the cogs so that every stage the whole thing fits together. Think of a watch that started out as a paperclip, and along the way became a pogo-stick. Think not of a watch that has and allways did have a single purpose, which was to tell the time. Think of a watch that once held sheets of paper together and could also be straightened out to form a toothpick, and which later turned out to be great for bouncing, and started to be used for measuring time only when someone noticed that it's rhythmic moments could be used to chart the passing seconds.
...
However, evolution need not merely add identifiable components like a factory worker assembling a machine. It can also remove them... or the entire structure can evolve in parallel.
....
Moreover, 'fail' is a slippery concept: a watch that lack hands is a failure at telling the time, but you can still use it to detonate a time-bomb, or hang it on a string to make a plumb-line. Organs and biochemical systems often change their functions often change their functions as they evolve, as we've just seen in the case of the flagellum and the eye [light-sensing function originally (possibly) came from bateria which converted light into energy, rather than into vision]

Quote: macaddict_17, 2007-04-06T20:00:53Z
1. The rate of decay has remained constant (The good one)
2. The system has remained closed (The bad one)
3. The ratio of daughter to parent in the rock is known (The ugly one)
I can name at least one other - Zirconium, that forms new 'layers' each time it remains in a high temperature/pressure environment for long enough, but is otherwise unchanged - and is unchanged by pretty much everything else.
Zircon crystals rise in mountains due to plate techtonics, then are eroded away, end up in the sea, are buried by sediment, form a new layer in the crystal due to the increased heat/pressure, and then are raised once more as the plates shift.
While new layers are forming, Uranium (and only uranium, as it alone is similar enough to zirconium (same atomic size/charge) to form impurities in the crystal) is incorporated into each new layer and then decays into lead as time passes. So... the system is closed and only uranium can initially be present. That's 2 and 3. Furthermore, the sequence also allows us to make a prediction about the crystals - that each layer further into the crystal will have a greater lead:uranium ratio, because the layers get older as you go deeper. That this prediction is correct (which it is) strongly supports the age of the crystal, and the reliability of this method of dating.

The oldest Zircon crystals are, dated by this method, 3.8 billion years old.

Quote: macaddict_17, 2007-04-13T15:39:28Z
And note that this is a unique dating system which seems to deal with #3 - most other systems accumulate the daughter product, and can be comprised of both in the initial rocks.
So? All that is needed is one reliable method of dating, and the earth must be at least that age. These 'unique' dating methods are just that.

Quote: macaddict_17, 2007-04-06T20:00:53Z
And as I stated before, you need more connecting lines, not just the dots.
You're asking for the impossible. And your metaphor really doesn't help you.
Think about a join-the-dots puzzle (which is a rather good metaphor for the scientific process, allthough a crossword is generally better). In it, you get a page with a set of dots on, and you have to connect those dots to form a coherent picture. In this particular case, each new fossil is a new dot on the paper, but there are never any lines. We fill the lines in ourselves - and we have done, to form the most coherent picture from the dots that we have. It may be in the future that as more dots are found the occasional line will have to be detoured to fit - and if we found an infinte number of fossils then the dots would merge together to form a line, a picture made entirely of dots, but until then all we can do is, as stated, do the best with what we've got. You're asking us for the 'infinite fossil' scenario. It's never going to happen.
Furthermore, every fossil is a transitional - between it's parents and it's offspring. If a different set of fossils - of 'dots' - had been found, a similar picture could still be drawn, and it would be close to the picture drawn now. But then you'd be asking for a new set of 'transitionals' - more of the filling-the-gaps.

"When The Origin Of Species was first published, the fossil record was poorly known. At that time, the complaint about the lack of transitional fossils bridging the major vertebrate taxa was perfectly reasonable. Opponents of Darwin's theory of common descent (the theory that evolution has occurred; not to be confused with the separate theory that evolution occurs specifically by natural selection) were justifiably skeptical of such ideas as birds being related to reptiles. The discovery of Archeopteryx only two years after the publication of The Origin of Species was seen a stunning triumph for Darwin's theory of common descent. Archeopteryx has been called the single most important natural history specimen ever found, "comparable to the Rosetta Stone" (Alan Feduccia, in "The Age Of Birds"). O.C. Marsh's groundbreaking study of the evolution of horses was another dramatic example of transitional fossils, this time demonstrating a whole sequence of transitions within a single family. Within a few decades after the Origin, these and other fossils, along with many other sources of evidence (such as developmental biology and biogeography) had convinced the majority of educated people that evolution had occurred, and that organisms are related to each other by common descent.
Since then, many more transitional fossils have been found, as sketched out in this FAQ. Typically, the only people who still demand to see transitional fossils are either unaware of the currently known fossil record (often due to the shoddy and very dated arguments presented in current creationist articles) or are unwilling to believe it for some reason."

And to expand the Stephen Gould quote from earlier - "The supposed lack of intermediary forms in the fossil record remains the fundamental canard of current antievolutionists. Such transitional forms are scarce, to be sure, and for two sets of reasons - geological (the gappiness of the fossil record) and biological (the episodic nature of evolutionary change, including patterns of punctuated equilibrium and transition within small populations of limited geological extenet). But paleontologists have discovered several superb examples of intermediary forms and sequences, more than enough to convince any fair-minded skeptic about the reality of life's physical geneology."

Quote: macaddict_17, 2007-04-24T21:43:01Z
It's science. It has a initial observations (Somebody killed this guy, Person A had a motive, so did Person B). It has hypotheses (Person A did it, because Person B has a reliable alibi). It has testing of the hypotheses (Do Person A's fingerprints appear on the murder weapon, or is it someone else?). And when the hypothesis is falsified, the experiment may be repeated, with the same or different fingerprints, or the hypothesis may be rejected.
Initial observations: several species alive today appear to share a dramatically similar body plan.
Hypothesis: Those species might share a common ancester/ancestral group.
Testing of the hypothesis: does DNA of todays creatures show any correlation with each other?
Repetition: Use different species, different DNA, etc...
OR
Initial observations: Darwins finches, mutating bacteria, breeding dogs/plants
Hypothesis: Evolution states that animals change over time
Testing hypothesis: Are there similarly-shaped fossils showing a sequence of change?
Repetition: use different species branches, lok for different similarities (nasal drift, tooth shape, shrinking/growing limbs)
Similarities?

#319793 434 2007-05-09T14:55:25Z iangb
Something has to be an object to physically exist. The wind does not physically exist, it is merely the name given to the consequence of an emergent system of molecules with a specific initial energy. Running, thinking and ethics are even harder to pin down - but they do not physically exist - they are concepts, nothing more. Without a sentient mind to observe them, to create them, they do not exist.

God does not physically exist. But God is outside of science and therefore this poses no problem to Him. The big question is - does God require sentient observation to exist, or can He observe Himself? Is He merely a concept, or is He a non-physical reality?
No-one can answer that one.

The proof I'm suprised no-one has used yet is a simple one. In it, (9) refferes to 'nine recurring'
  1. x = 0.(9)
  2. 10x = 9.(9)
  3. 9x = 10x - x = 9.(9) - 0.(9) = 9
  4. x = 9/9 = 1
  5. 0.(9) = x = 1
  6. 0.(9) = 1
0.(9) is mathematically identical to 1. Physically, infinity does not exist (Kablizzy, a black hole is definitely not an example of infinity - it still has a finite mass, even if that mass still is stunningly huge) so this point is moot, but mathematically that's the way it is.

It's Last Thursdayism.

I've said this before, but I'll say it again now. Just as in forensics, you have to take all the evidence that is available to you and you have to make the most plausible, the most simple (Occams razor, in a way) situation out of the evidence available. If you look at the evidence so far, you can break it down three ways:

Evidence for an old Earth: All.
Evidence for a young earth: All, given that a Designer played around a bit
Evidence for YEC: All, given that God played around a bit and that the Bible is correct, and all the other loopholes intrinsic to the bible.

If you assume divine interference, you could beleive that all the clouds on Earth are pink, but God makes everyone see them as non-pink. Or that gravity does not exist, and it's just the Flying Spaghetti Monster holding us down with His Noodly Appendages. Or that light has been travelling for only 6000 years, but was placed in-flight 6000 years ago so humanity could navigate the globe.

And I'll also say this again. The only evidence for a six-thousand-year-old earth is in the literal interpretation of the bible. Because, going back to Last Thursdayism, if things can appear older than they are, what's to stop them being no more than a few days, weeks, even a few miliseconds old?

Quote: R.A.Salvatore @ Icewind Dale Trilogy
I pray that the world never runs out of dragons. I say that in all sincerity, though I have played a part in the death of one great wyrm. For the dragon is the quintessential enemy, the greatest foe, the unconquerable epitome of devastation. The dragon, above all other creatures, even the demons and the devils, evokes images of dark grandeur, of the greatest beast curled asleep on the greatest treasure hoard. They are the ultimate test of he hero and the ultimate fright of the child. They are older than the elves and more akin to the earth than the dwarves. The great dragons are the preternatural beast, the basic element of the beast, that darkest part of our imagination.

The wizards cannot tell you of their origin, though they believe that a great wizard, a god of wizards, must have played some role in the first spawning of the beast. The elves, with their long fables explaining the creation of every aspect of the world, have many ancient tales concerning the origin of the dragons, but they admit, privately, that they really have no idea of how the dragons came to be.
My own belief is more simple, and yet, more complicated by far. I believe that dragons appeared in the world immediately after the spawning of the first reasoning race. I do not credit any god of wizards with their creation, but rather, the most basic imagination wrought of unseen fears, of those first reasoning mortals.

We make the dragons as we make the gods, because we need them, because, somewhere deep in our hearts, we recognize that a world without them is a world not worth living in.

There are so many people in the land who want an answer, a definitive answer, for everything in life, and even for everything after life. They study and they test, and because those few find the answers for some simple questions, they assume that there are answers to be had for every question. What was the world like before there were people? Was there nothing but darkness before the sun and the stars? Was there anything at all? What were we, each of us, before we were born? And what, most importantly of all, shall we be after we die?

Out of compassion, I hope that those questioners never find that which they seek.

One self-proclaimed prophet came through Ten-Towns denying the possibility of an afterlife, claiming that those people who had died and where raised by priests, had, in fact, never died, and that their claims of experiences beyond the grave were an elaborate trick played on them by their own hearts, a ruse to ease the path to nothingness. For that is all there was, he said, an emptiness, a nothingness.

Never in my life have I ever heard one begging so desperately for someone to prove him wrong.
For what are we left with if there remains no mystery? What hope might we find if we know all of the answers?

What is it within us, then, that so desperately wants to deny magic and to unravel mystery? Fear, I presume, based on the many uncertainties of life and the greatest uncertainty of death. Put those fears aside, I say, and live free of them, for if we just step back and watch the truth of the world, we will find that there is indeed magic all about us, unexplainable by numbers and formulas. What is the passion evoked by the stirring speech of the commander before the desperate battle, if not magic? What is the peace that an infant might know in its mothers arms, if not magic? What is love, if not magic?

No, I would not want to live in a world without dragons, as I would not want to live in a world without magic, for that is a world without mystery, and that is a world without faith.

And that, I fear, for any reasoning, conscious being, would be the cruelest trick of all.

-Drizzt DoUrden

False assumptions about radiometric dating have lead some scientists to believe that the world is old. On the contrary, if one rejects these false assumptions, the world does not look old.
I take it you mean the 'false' assumption that the rock formed naturally, and without any sort of divine interference. Because if the rock formed naturally, there is no way that impurities would be present - for reasons I stated a few pages back.
From a purely scientific viewpoint, radiometric dating is accurate. You need divine interference to make it innaccurate: but luckilly for you, you've got that. My point is, that if God can make things appear older than they are (for example, Adam and Eve were not created as babies, so they appeared to be older than they were) then why use any scientific method to date the earth? Which, essentially, is Omphalos.

Also, if God made the rocks initially impure, He really did deliberately make them 'old'. Several dating techniques (well, technically the same technique applied to different decay chains) look not just at the initial and terminal steps of a decay chain, but at every element in that chain. This technique is even better than the one listed before, because any impurities anywhere down the decay chain would result in a deviation from the exected values:
If you imagine a graph of the amount of different decay daughters (and grand-daugters, etc, etc) present in a rock that changed with time, starting from a pure parent sample would give a completely predictable multi-point graph at any point in time, from which the age of the rock could be calculated. Any variation in initial purity of the sample would then become obvious in the graph, as a deviation from the expected that continues down the chain: so if the chain went A-->B-->C-->D-->E then an initial impurity of C would affect the recorded values of C, D and E so that they were different from expected.
So, for a rock to appear older than expected from this techniqe, it would need appropriatly valued impurities of every single element in the decay chain with a relevant half-life. That's not something that happens accidentally.

Quote: macaddict_17, 2007-05-25T19:07:14Z
What could possibly be more in conflict with the Laws of Thermodynamics than your last statement? I hate to break it to you, Ian, but much of what I've been saying here has been something of a lure, trying to get you to say outright that with time, chance beats humans in complexity. (This is as close as I'm gonna get, so here goes).
Note that I said 'given time'.
I did make a mistake, in that I should have reffered to chance as part of an emergent system: again, chance constrained by rules, as in the formation of snowdrops. With rules added, thermodynamics becomes a little... hazy (this, incidentally, is rather good revision for my thermodnamics test in a month or so).

For one thing, thermodynamics without constraint can form paradoxes - like the Gibbs paradox. Also, it is incresingly hard to define 'order' or 'chaos'. Imagine a system initially comprised of semi-diffusely spread black holes, and a identical system (on a much smaller scale) comprised of a cluster of semi-diffusely spread air particles. As time passes, the black hole system will end up with a single supermassive black hole - effectively all the particles clustered around a point. The air-particle system, however, will end up as a totally diffused set of particles. In both cases, standard physical rules have applied, but with vastly different outcomes - if thermodynamicsII is true, then both outcomes have maximised external entropy. And yet the two oucomes are opposites.
Defining 'order' is a little... tricky. And don't get me started on statistical quantum thermodynamics.

Would you say snowflakes break the law? After all, they are formed by chance. And now they're helping us design better microchips.

The answer to any paradox.
Quote
Miss Tangerine was one of the faster-learning Auditors and had already formulated a group of things, events, and situations that she categorized as "bloody stupid." Things that were "bloody stupid" could be dismissed.

My latest paradox is the Gibbs paradox, which pokes holes in classical thermodynamics (may be slightly technical if you don't understand the concept of entropy). Essentially: if you mix gas A and gas B then chaos has increaced; there is now a mixture of gas AB which if you arbitrarily split in two you would never get two pure samples of A and B back.
However, if gas B is the same as gas A, then after the positive entropy change of the mixing there is no increace in chaos - if you arbitrarily divided the gas AA in two then you would get back two pure smples of gas A. That means negative entropy, which breaks thermodynamics somewhat.

jeez, I'm a nerd.

#329210 13 2007-06-09T15:27:08Z iangb
There is no concept of the present. We're living in the past.

I mean it. The smallest length of time something has been measured over is on the attosecond scale (10^-18 seconds), so if there is an ultimate minimum length it is less than an attosecond long. In one attosecond, even light travels a mere 3*10^-10 metres, and nerve impulses are far slower - using the max value of 119m/s it would take a whopping 15*10^15 attoseconds (15 milliseconds) for the signal that you've just trodden on a pin to reach your brain. Add onto that reaction time, and humans live just behind the ever-moving 'now' - essentially we live on our memories. That possibly explains a lot about us.

#330846 14 2007-06-13T15:10:52Z iangb
Oh dear. Maestro is right, pretty much everyone else is wrong.

ASCII is the method, amongst other things, by which the keyboard communicates with the processor. It is a code where each individual symbol (printable ones like $ or non-printable ones like carriage return) is represented by a number.

ASCII art is pictures made with nothing but those encodeable characters.

Binary is a counting system in base 2 (normally nubers are counted in base 10) - it uses 1 and 0 only to make any number.

Alt Numbers are another type of encoding, similar to ASCII but different. Use the method described above to use them.

Sorted?

#354296 6 2007-08-12T00:12:53Z iangb
Horray, horray, here comes another quantum!

Yeah, I was on a brief haitus of apathy. I'll be back in a week or so, as I'm spending most of next week in a field trying not to swear at camping scouts.

The rate of radioactive decay can be likened to your standard exothermal reaction in chemistry. In such a reaction, the two reactants lose energy, becoming more stable. However, they often need a certain 'activation energy' to get started. Budding chemists quickly learn that to make a reaction happen you often have to heat it up: this gives the reactants the energy to react, so stuff happens.
For radioactive decay, heating the element will have no effect. Instead, the 'activation energy' required is received from quantum vacuum fluctuations (in laymans terms, spacetime spontaniously 'frothing' on a really tiny scale). This is in turn is a direct consequence of (or, more precisely, is described very well by) the Heisenburg uncertanty principle, which states that the uncertainty in the combined measurement of momentum (read: energy) and position of an object can never be less than (h/4[pi]). h is the Planck constant, which has been proven to be the same since pretty much the start of the universe.

So. Plancks constant is time-independant (it is the same regardless of when it is measured). This means that the Uncertainty Principle is equally time-independant (as all it includes is position, momentum and h). This means that the decay rate of a particular element is time-independant, as is the half-life. It all works.
