#357064 16 2007-08-19T12:46:23Z iangb
Age of the earth - this is, indeed, due to rocks. Zircon crystals are amazingly resiliant rocks - they are formed in lava, pushed up into granite mountatains via tectonic plate movements, and end up back in the lava again as the mountain erodes and is slowly washed out to sea. Each time (in this cycle) that the crystal is in the lava it aquires a new outer shell containing (amongst other things) particles of uranium, but is otherwise unchanged. The uranium then decays in its closed environment, so the time at which each layer was laid down can be found using radiometric dating. This means that zircon crystals today have shells which are younger on the outside and older on the inside. Some of the inside shells are very old indeed.
Also, see The Age of the Earth (wiki).

Age of the universe - Atilla said. Also, Wiki knows all again

I'm going to make an assumption about how you think, Suki, and then go from there. If the first idea is wrong the rest will surely be; feel free to trip me up before I get started. This might ramble a bit, as well.

How Tsukatu Thinks
To be good at anything, you need to be logically consistent. Any tautologies you subscribe to (as fundamental axioms) have to be absolute. So, to be a 'good' Christian, you need to totally beleive in God - and the only two ways to learn about God are the Bible and in the teachings of the Church, so you have to fully beleive in them, too. Clearly, if there is a perceived disagreement between the church's teachings and the bible, the bible should reign supreme, because to be a Christian you have to beleive that the Bible is handed down from God, and the human Church is more open to corruption than a book written by divine inspiration. So far, all is fine and dandy.
However, the Bible contradicts itself. It also (when taken literally, which is how it needs to be taken) results in massive conflicts with science (read: reality). As such, Christianity as a whole is logically incorrect. Any so-called 'Christians' who don't follow the bible literally may have found resolution for themselves, but they are no longer true Christians because they are no longer following the Bible to the letter, and as such can be ignored when considering 'Christianity' as a whole.
The true Christians therefore tend to fundamentalist ways; which are harmfull to humanity in general (see the Westborough baptist church, spanish inquisition, specific examples of church-led oppresion of scientific progress, and so on). Add to that what they beleive can't be true (due to logical inconsistancies with the bible/YEC vs Evolution, etc... I'm still interested in if you can justify this as a bad thing, incidentally) and that any conflicts between science and religion must end (due to the fundamental axiom of the bible) with blind faith leading the way, and you are drawn to the undeniable conclusion that Christianity is nothing but harmful to humanity and deserves extinction.

I have to admit, this is quite a lot of 'How Ian though a few years ago' superimposed onto Tsukatu, supported by what he's been writing so far. Now for the tricky bit, in which I try not to sound like an evangelist.

Why Tsukatu Is Wrong (aka Ian saying why he beleives what he beleives. Again. Sorry, McP)
To be a good Christian, you need to beleive in God. But (and this is the important bit), God is unknowable. As such, you cannot use anything as absolute truth, because you have no guarentee that it is correct - it might just be another mysterious way in which God moves. You can use the teachings of the church and of the bible as hints on the mind of God, but never as absolute fact. And this opens up a whole other realm of possibilities, and turns Christianity into much more of a science in it's own right (alebeit a science with a driving faith) - because you can use the world around you as another way of getting hints - after all, if someone made everything, you can learn about the creator by studying the creation. I don't mean looking for Jesus appearing on a slice of toast, instead you can (for example) see God introduce evolution, and then beat biological evolution with social evolution, and you can infer that if biological evolution was to produce humanity (amongst other things), social evolution muct also have been to introduce 'correct' society (morals/ethics), although whether we've got there or not is another question. You might be wrong, but if it helps you live a good life does it really matter? And if you are in the minority that does take the Bible literally, that's just another way of viewing Christianity. It's not the defining thing.


Of course, that still requires a beleif in God to drive the whole thing. But that's the only choice - to take the path of a Christian scientist is perfectly viable. You just have to accept God's almost utter unknowablity.
You could say that the fundamental axiom of the atheist is empiricism/logic, the fundamental axiom of the theist is God. Beyond that choice the reasoning works both ways.

http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fusion_power

Now, I'm really interested to understand what the hell they're talking about, but I don't understand it because I'm an uneducated little human. All I get out of it is that we can get a whole lot of energy from two nuclei being fused together, and this fusion reactor creates heat 10 times hotter than the core of the sun. Is there any way you can explain this in simpler terms?
Uh... only sort of. I can say the basic ideas again, in simpler words, though.

Nuclear fusion is, essentially, when two seperate atomic nuclei combine to form a single, larger, atomic nucleus. The physics behind that bit is deceptively simple - there are two important forces at work; electromagnetism and the 'strong nuclear force'. Because a nucleus is made up of protons (+ve charge) and neutrons (no charge), every nucleus has a positive electromagnetic charge. This means that over almost every distance, two nuclei will repel each other (like repels like). However, the 'strong nuclear force' is a much stronger attractive force, but it only works across a much shorter range. So if you can get two nuclei close enough to each other, the strong nuclear force will overcome the electromagnetic force and the two nucleii will stick together.
If you can get them to stick together, they tend to briefly form an unstable heavy nucleus, which then (in laymans terms) 'explodes' into two seperate, stable bits - generally a heavy nucleus and a single neutron. Because these components are more 'stable' (sorry, laymans terms again) than the starting nuclei, a lot of energy is produced in the 'explosion'.
At the moment, the only way to get a fusion reaction to take place is with immense heat and pressure - fusion reactions occur in the sun (which is noted for it's high temperature) and inside the blast from a hydrogen bomb - the first reaction is set off by a seperate method, and then the explosion feeds itself (energy from the first reaction sparks the nexts, and so on). However, experiments are being carried out to try and use a controlled form of fusion as an energy source - using superheated plasma (charged gas) suspended in a magnetic field as fuel. So far, it's been unsuccesfull, but theres a large test reactor being built that might just work. We'll see.

Quote: Twistkill, 2006-03-19T02:05:16Z

Why does the evolution theory say we evolved from monkeys? If we did, why do monkeys still exist today?

I don't feel this was addressed enough. I'm sure you well know now that humans didn't come from monkeys; I'm not talking about that.

Let's say that A evolved from B. The fact that A and B both exist today is not a valid argument against evolution. Evolution full well permits it.

In the world where only A existed, there was competition, as there always is among organisms, and the ones who had a mutation that made them closer to B were better able to compete, so they survived. (Keep in mind that the mutated version of the species survives only if it can copulate more than the original verson.) However, those B's only have that advantage in the particular environment in which the B-mutation was developed. From here, there are several answers to the question "why do A's still exist":
-A's are still able to survive and copulate. They may not be as good as B's, but they're still competent and can keep reproducing.
-A's may exist in other parts of the world in environments where the B-mutation never developed.
-A's may exist in other parts of the world in environments where the B-mutation was either not an advantage, or was even a disadvantage.
-The B-mutation may have forced the affected portion of the species to migrate, and create an environment composed of B's, leaving the A's in the original environment.
I don't know if twistkill still holds his original views, but...

I have nothing more to add.

One of the arguments against the 'If I don't observe something it doesn't exist' worldview is that it is something of an arrogant statement to make. Why should the existence of an external universe rely on the existance of someone to observe it? Furthermore, why should that 'someone' be 'me'?

If I fall over in the forest and you aren't there to see me, will I make a sound? The obvious answer (unless you're feeling particularly sollipistic) is: yes. Is there really a difference between this situation and the tree situation? Technically: no. Me 'hearing' the noise as I crash to the floor is simply the result of particles of air interacting with the particles in my ear. My presence does not affect the existence of the particles of air; otherwise you would have some sort of horrific (backwards?) causality, where the tree 'knows' whether I am present or not and 'decides' whether or not to make the air particles vibrate.


The biggest piece of evidence for the tree being in the interim state of 'falling' is that if it wasn't, then it would not have been obeying physical laws. If it wasn't obeying physical laws, then there is no reason for the tree to be lying down like that as if it had. Why has it not spontaniously turned a rather fetching shade of blue?
While you cannot absolutely prove the consistency of physical laws under non-observation, you need a conspiracy theory to explain the alternative.

#390959 46 2007-12-19T03:02:19Z iangb
In that thread, my argument that got shot down is now strangely relevant again, because we are starting with the assumption that free will exists in life. To recap it here:

Global premise 0: God exists, is omnibenevolent and omnipotent (but constrained, for the moment, by logic and free will).
Global premise 1: Heaven exists, and is a perfect place free from suffering.
Global premise 2: Free will exists in (at least) life
Argument 1: Free will is given by God because He loves us. Therefore free will is a good thing - life with free will is preferable to life without free will. Therefore free will exists in heaven, as life in heaven without free will is less preferable to life with free will, and heaven is perfect.
Argument 2: Free will directly causes suffering. This is proved by contradiction: if it did not, then God could use his omnipotency to ensure everyone lived suffering-free lives without breaking His constraint under the soverignty of free will. Therefore there is no free will in heaven, as heaven is free from suffering.
Obviously, arguments one and two are contradictory. This means (assuming both arguments are watertight) that one or more of the three premises is incorrect. Looking at them, in reverse order:
2. Heaven does not exist. This causes problems in that Heaven is one of the core beleifs of Christianity.
1. Free will does not exist in life. This raises the old problem of suffering in life vs an omnibenevolent god.
0. God does not exist. Crap.

The other solution, of course, is that God is omnipotent about the whole thing: He may agree to be bound by free will and allow free will in heaven, but as He is not constrained by logic then He can solve all problems without breaking his self-imposed boundaries, even though this is logically impossible. However, there are related issues with this: as this solution is arrived at through nothing but logic, but it concerns an illogical God and is therefore inherantly flawed. (see the 'Logic and ineffability' thread).

Quote: Obby, 2007-12-20T23:35:15Z
That's not how chance and probability work. You do not group the odds of an event together with other events. On a much simpler scale, it's like this; I roll a die. I have a one in six chance that I roll a 2. The next time I roll the die, I have the same chances. This does not mean that after I roll the die 2 times, I should have rolled 2 2's. Each individual roll is separate. It is equally correct (or incorrect) to say that I will always or never roll a 2. So in this universe, vastness is not a realistic argument. Each second that passes, the chances are the same. (One in a hundred thousand trillion trillion trillion trillion trillion trillion trillion trillion trillion trillion.) Technically, an amino acid could be formed every second, because there is a chance, albeit a small one. Then again, is also technically alright to say that an amino acid could never be formed. It goes either way.

Anyways, my point is that you can not group probability together. Each chance must be treated as an individual event. You'd be surprised how often the actual results differ from the probability. (I can personally guarantee that I rolled about 6 6's last week in monopoly, even though I only rolled about 25 times.
Woo, I get to say (a warped version of) it again!

Learn some probability.

If there is a small chance of somethin happening, vastness is a good argument to deal with the problem. Here comes the math...

Say, for simplicities sake, that the chance is a tiny 0.001% likelyhood, and the event occurs a million times. To rephrase this, the chance of the event not occuring once is 0.99999 (out of 1), so the chance of it not occuring in the million times is 0.99999^1000000.

0.99999^1000000 = 4.53976485 10^-5, or 0.0000454 , or 0.005%. Even though there was a minute chance of the event occuring, repeating the experiment a vast number of times leads to the event being incredibly likely to occur.

I can see this now turning into an argument about the nature of causation, so I'll (try to) step in.

One description of 'causation' is that "A causes B because if the scenario was run again with every aspect the same other than the presence of A, B would not occur". This makes sense: if free will did not cause suffering, then what did? Lucifer? But He was only excercising his free will in tempting humanity. If He had no free will, he would not have been able to cause the suffering in the first place.

Thus, free will incontrevertibly caused suffering. The big question is: would free will always cause suffering? I think it would, because in order for no suffering to be caused, every minute choice made by every human would have to be the 'correct' one. If we have no option but to make the 'correct' choice, then we don't really have free will. (Or our lives are severely controlled, which some might describe as 'suffering' in any case).

Very well, lets look at 2 Kings 1, 2 Kings 2 and 2 Kings 3, in a search for higher context. It's certainly interesting reading.


2 Kings 1 describes how Elijah pronounces doom on a king for consulting with "Baal-zebub, the God of Ekon". The king sends three groups of 50 soldiers to take Elijah to speak with the king: Elisha kills the first two groups with fire from heaven and then, due to an intervention of the Angel, goes with the third soldiers and pronounces doom once more. Accordingly, the king dies.
2 Kings 2 describes how Elijah is taken to God in a whirlwind. His succesor, Elisha, who followed Elijah up until that point, then heals a fouled spring and kills 42 youths with a bear.
2 Kings 3 describes how Israel crushes the Moab rebellion, partly due to Elisha irrigating a desert and filling the ditches with water, enabling the Israli army to survive long enough to fight.

So. Apart from the fact that there is more God-based killing in 2 Kings 1, there is no context whatsoever for the 42 youths (nor is there any in the rest of 2 Kings, I merely can't be bothered to post summaries of all 22 chapters). Feel free to provide some.

I've browsed 4chan, on and off, for the past 3 to 4 years, and been down to some pretty hellish places myself out of morbid curiosity. I know that it's a shithole, and that the users united in pursuit of chaos is multiple tragedy, and that the internet has some unplumbably dark corners (which I doubt either of us has seen clear to the bottom of). I know that a majority of Anonymous is in it for the lulz, and that this essentially started as a larger version of ebaums vs YTMND. A large portion of what you've said: I agree with. Specifically, that this is not, and hopefully never will be, /b/. Because that would be bad.

That said, there are some things I don't agree with. The fact that because anon is, well, anonymous doesn't mean that I should treat every member as if they were the worst sort of /b/tard. There are billions of people in this world who will forever remain anonymous to me, and some of them will do and have done terrible things, both on a collective and an individual scale. That doesn't mean that I should treat any new person I meet as if they are a child molester; nor should I treat the group 'everyone who I haven't met yet' with the same disregard. Some irish friends of mine got into a fight at the weekend: I shouldn't label the entire country as 'violent'. A paper aeroplane is thrown at the teacher: she shouldn't punish the whole class.

Another thing that grates is the suggestion that /b/ could spill over into real life (or elseswhere, eg here). As you've said, neither of us know what could happen. The only evidence we've had so far of anon in RL is the demonstrations that went down worldwide a few days ago, and while there was the occasional meme flung about there was absolutely minimal violence (given that in any crowd of random protesters you will get a fight sooner or later; as far as I could tell there were one or two minor scuffles that couldn't be connected to the protesters) and even less disorderly conduct. Looking at the enturbulation forums while the protests were going on showed a group of people trying to minimise the /b/-ness for the sake of spreading a public message.
The difference between /b/ and everywhere else is, as you've stated, that /b/ has absolutely minimal rules (CP is deleted when found, and never encouraged, even by the majority of Anon themselves). But the fact that /b/ is lawless doesn't mean that the rest of the world has to change. Although there have been some/several/many raids to other forums and the like, /b/ can only find a foothold to work outside the law where there is guilabillity or weakness. That just means that you can't allow this forum to be weak or guillable; something which I'm fairly sure it isn't. In RL, where there are far more serious consequences and anonymity is fairly impossible, the spread of chaos is severely limited.

In a cunning link, I think that scientology is the greater of two evils. Not specifically because of the harm it's done, but because it used the legal system to acheive it. The very fact that a corporation can be allowed to dominate and get away with it simply on the grounds that 'it is a religion' is one that needs to be stamped out, the sooner the better. If it gives some randomer a few lulz because it adds some chaos to their world, so be it. Even if inspires them to more RL activities, I'm not too bothered: for the RL demonstrators to make that much effort shows (to me at least) that they actually were in it for more than just lulz: they had some sort of cause, even if the original motivation for finding said cause was something petty and insignificant and lulz-related.

While you've seen the exponential growth of 'anonymous', the growth on /b/ has been minimal, at best. The post rate is unchanged, and I haven't seen any CoS-related threads so far today. For /b/, at least, the fad is fading until the next oppertunity for lulz. Enturbulation, on the other hand, is still going strong. Doesn't that imply that this has spiraled beyond the core of 4chan?

You misunderstood what I mean about meme-spreading. Memes will naturally spread: that's their function. You've been borrowing 4chan ones, above, and I'm doing the same a little. But 4chan isn't trying to expand itself. Forum raiders don't go out with the intention of recruiting, they go out with the intention of mischeif, chaos and disruption. The CoS, on the other hand, is. And I'd rather see a horsecock as my homepage than be sued for infringing religious freedom: the worst case endpoints for both (as I am also neither guillable nor particularly weak).

Why were you banning 4chan here? Because you're terrified of these forums becoming /b/. But (as stated above), /b/ is chaotic because it's rule-less. There's nothing wrong with allowing memes: the ones that are pointless/offensive will be taken away by the spam/flaming rules anyway, which is what differentiates us from them. You're confusing 'let people say tl;dr -' with 'remove all of the rules and let the members run wild'.

Can you elaborate on what you mean by the paragraph just under your 'blizzblag' quote? As far as I can see, you're confusing our argument with Obby's (why protest X when Y is worse). We banned people because they broke the rules: regardless of what those rules were. McP got exactly the same punishment as Chonnymon.





tl;dr - While I accept that /b/ as a collective contains jackasses and worse, I don't believe that Anonymous is entirely, wholely or singularly /b/. Nor do I believe that a subsection of /b/ or individuals of /b/ should be treated as the bad individuals would be treated: this is prejudice (memism?), allowing the actions of one part of a group to overrule my opinion of the group as a whole. I do believe, however, that the CoS is worth the effort and the consequences of raising public awareness over, even though the original snub was something petty and insignificant. I do not agree with any of the illegal activities of Anonymous. Finally, I do not believe that this forum will ever become /b/, due to the strong staff and existence of rules.

#426807 11 2008-04-10T14:23:51Z iangb
Unfortunately though, scythe, it does come back to nuclear. 'Cos although hydrogen burns cleanly, getting the hydrogen is a whole 'nother matter.

Of the three main methods of hydrogen production, two (hydrocarbons and algae) both produce CO2, so in order to make the production method greenhouse-friendly, you need to use carbon capture - something which
a) Could also be used with the burning of fossil fuels (though more specifically at power stations that at-the-car, currently)
b) I'm highly dubious about. Carbon capture is essentially taking CO2 that is released and storing it underground... for ever. It's the greenhouse gas equivalent of a landfill site, and look how successful those have been.

The third method of production is electrolysis of water: something which doesn't cause any pollutants in itself (much like the combustion of hydrogen), but which requires electricity to do so - essentially the energy from the electricity is being used to power the car, just via the medium of hydrogen. In order for that electricity to be 'clean', we need to address the problem of power stations. Enter conventional nuclear (a short-term stopgap), solar/wave/tidal/geothermal power (our best current option, IMO), and fast breeder reactors (th3 f00tur3, as Keron would put it)

#19958 1 2008-04-16T14:28:05Z iangb
[Here's the deal. I'm writing a philosophy essay soon entitled 'Responses to the Problem of Induction'. While I know what I want to say, I'm intrigued to know what the general reaction to this problem is. So if you feel like it, read the problem through, and post me your response(s). Feel free to go look up stuff if you want, but I'm most interested in your instinctive response, as there are some bog-standard replies to the problem.]

Firstly, you need to know what the problem of induction is. For that, you need to know what induction itself is, so we'll start there and work onwards.

Induction is the line of reasoning which is formalised by the scientific method, but which is also the method by which everyone lives their everyday lives. Essentially, induction can be phrased thusly: "If it's always behaved in a certain way, it will continue to behave in a certain way". We know from past experience that gravity has always pulled stuff downwards, and we expect it to continue to do so while we play basketball. We know that biting into an apple will taste nice (assuming you like apples, natch), and this knowledge of past experiences influences our future choices when we go shopping. Induction is why we are so surprised by magic tricks - they break our expectations as to how we think objects 'should' behave. All science does is formalise this relationship and describe more mathematically/quantitatively how things appear to work.

In short, if anyone asks you why, when they drop a rock, it falls to the ground, your inductive answer will be "because that is what always happens".

So, onwards to the problem of induction*. You must ask yourself 'how do we know that induction is a valid line of reasoning?' The answer sounds disturbingly familiar: "because induction has always given valid predictions" - in other words, "because induction working is what always happens". As this shows, the justification for 'believing' in induction is induction itself. This means that induction is a tautology (a self-supporting argument) and there is no reason for using it. The consequences of this are huge - not only that science is baseless, but that there is no reason for us to expect our everyday assumptions to be true. Because of this problem, there is no reason _whatsoever_ for believing that the sun will rise tomorrow.

I welcome your responses.

* In fact, there are a couple of other problems with induction, mainly involving black swans or the colour grue. I won't go into them here, unless I get really bored later this month.

Quote: DemonzLunchBreak, 2008-04-17T02:14:34Z
Karl Popper tried to solve the problem of induction. You might want to have a look at his work, Ian. Then again, I don't think what he proposes is really a solution. It's more of a way of avoiding the problem.
Heh, been there, done that, and I don't particularly like it. Popper tried to claim that the scientific method/day-to-day reasoning does not use induction at all, instead it logically comes up with a hypothesis, and then logically tests that hypothesis against observable 'reality' to see if it is valid or not. However, Poppers view makes it impossible to make any predictions about the future: you can only use it to explain that which has already happened. To make predictions still either requires inductive thinking, or a re-asking of the question "how do you know that a theory which has held true up until now will continue to hold true?".

#449993 16 2008-07-01T17:43:16Z iangb
There are two things that will be affected by increaced gun control laws.

Gun ownership will go down, so there will be less illegal gun use. There will be a correlation between reduction in legal gun ownership and illegal gun ownership, because the total reduced number of firearms makes it easier to investigate individual firearm owners to see if their weapon is legal or not. Gun control laws only work if they are enforced, but when the enforcement is present, they work well (see study here). The pro-gun side tends to concentrate on the consequences of making the law and not enforcing it, which is (IMO) fairly unrealistic.

The other consequence is that gun ownership will go down, so there will be less legal gun use. So - less people will use a firearm to protect themselves from harm. Adverse effects from this may be less than predicted, however, because there are several non-lethal alternatives for personal defence - the Tazer springs to mind. However, injuries/fatalities that could be prevented by a firearm are clearly not a good thing.

The question then becomes - which will be affected more - illegal gun use, or legal gun use? At the moment, I'm leaning towards the illegal-gun-use-being-affected-more, because although a higher proportion of (currently) legal firearms will be removed from circulation, illegal arms use is faaaar higher than legal (1,2, 3, 4). However, there isn't really enough evidence to say either way. See here.

Traditional agnosticism is a subset of atheism.
This one again?

As far as I'm aware, 'atheism' and 'agnosticism' are in two entirely different categories. (A)theism is whether belief in god exists or not, whereas (a)gnosticism refers the the certainty about the belief. So - a gnostic theist would claim to have personally experienced God, whereas an agnostic atheist would not believe but would not be certain that (s)he is correct.

#452980 2 2008-07-15T10:11:15Z iangb
Yes.

I don't particularly understand the question. The universe contains the cosmos by definition, and it is a chaotic system - tiny changes now could have massive effects later. I'm guessing your question is 'Is the universe ordered or is it in chaos?' I can answer that one.

The universe is an ordered system, obeying physical rules (most of it... black holes are a special case, but it is likely that there are physical rules governing them, we just don't know what they are yet). However, the Universe is a chaotic system - meaning, as stated above, that tiny changes in today's system can have profound effects on the state of the system in the distant future. There are no particular consequences to this, other than that we should be fairly confident that the universe won't turn into a giant blancmange any time soon - the timescale of chaos is too large for it to make much difference to our mayfly lives. It does make tracking incoming meteors/comets a bit more interesting, though...
